column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>In multimedia applications, the text and image components in a web document form a pairwise constraint that potentially indicates the same semantic concept.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>This paper studies cross-modal learning via the pairwise constraint and aims to find the common structure hidden in different modalities.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We first propose a compound regularization framework to address the pairwise constraint, which can be used as a general platform for developing cross-modal algorithms.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>For unsupervised learning, we propose a multi-modal subspace clustering method to learn a common structure for different modalities.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>For supervised learning, to reduce the semantic gap and the outliers in pairwise constraints, we propose a cross-modal matching method based on compound ℓ21 regularization.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Extensive experiments demonstrate the benefits of joint text and image modeling with semantically induced pairwise constraints, and they show that the proposed cross-modal methods can further reduce the semantic gap between different modalities and improve the clustering/matching accuracy.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper shows how to link text and images by finding shared hidden patterns. The authors build a new mathematical framework and use it to create two tools: one that groups text and images without labels, and another that matches them when labels are present. Their tests prove these tools work better at reducing mistakes and improving accuracy in combining text and image data.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Developing complex engineered systems (CES) poses significant challenges for engineers, managers, designers, and businesspeople alike due to the inherent complexity of the systems and contexts involved.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Furthermore, experts have expressed great interest in filling the gap in theory about how CES develop.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>This article begins to address that gap in two ways.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>First, it reviews the numerous definitions of CES along with existing theory and methods on CES development processes.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Then, it proposes the ComplEx System Integrated Utilities Model (CESIUM), a novel framework for exploring how numerous system and development process characteristics may affect the performance of CES.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>CESIUM creates simulated representations of a system architecture, the corresponding engineering organization, and the new product development process through which the organization designs the system.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>It does so by representing the system as a network of interdependent artifacts designed by agents.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Agents iteratively design their artifacts through optimization and share information with other agents, thereby advancing the CES toward a solution.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>This paper describes the model, conducts a sensitivity analysis, provides validation, and suggests directions for future study.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: CESIUM is a new tool that copies how both a complicated machine and the team building it work together. It treats the machine as a web of parts, and the engineers as agents who share ideas and improve their designs. The authors ran tests in different situations to make sure CESIUM gives reliable results. Finally, they suggested ways other researchers could build on their work.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Remote attestation (RA) authenticates code running in trusted execution environments (TEEs), allowing trusted code to be deployed even on untrusted hosts.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>However, trust relationships established by one component in a distributed application may impact the security of other components, making it difficult to reason about the security of the application as a whole.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Furthermore, traditional RA approaches interact badly with modern web service design, which tends to employ small interacting microservices, short session lifetimes, and little or no state.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>This paper presents the Decent Application Platform, a framework for building secure decentralized applications.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Decent applications authenticate and authorize distributed enclave components using a protocol based on self-attestation certificates, a reusable credential based on RA and verifiable by a third party.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Components mutually authenticate each other not only based on their code, but also based on the other components they trust, ensuring that no transitively-connected components receive unauthorized information.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>While some other TEE frameworks support mutual authentication in some form, Decent is the only system that supports mutual authentication without requiring an additional trusted third party besides the trusted hardware's manufacturer.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We have verified the secrecy and authenticity of Decent application data in ProVerif, and implemented two applications to evaluate Decent's expressiveness and performance: DecentRide, a ride-sharing service, and DecentHT, a distributed hash table.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>On the YCSB benchmark, we show that DecentHT achieves 7.5x higher throughput and 3.67x lower latency compared to a non-Decent implementation.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: The Decent Application Platform is a new system that lets different pieces of a distributed app check each other’s code and make sure it’s safe—all without extra middlemen. Each piece uses a special digital “badge” (called a self-attestation certificate) plus mathematical proofs to keep data private and prove it’s genuine. Engineers tested it in real apps, like a ride-sharing service and a distributed hash table. In those tests, it ran about seven times faster than usual systems and made each response in less than a third of the time.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <CONTRIBUTION>New relations among the mixture direct correlation function integrals (or fluctuation integrals) in terms of concentration variables are developed.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>These relations indicate that, for example, for a binary mixture only one of the three direct correlation function integrals (or one of the three fluctuation integrals) is independent.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Different closure expressions for mixture cross direct correlation function integrals are suggested and they are joined with the exact relations to calculate all the direct correlation function integrals and fluctuation integrals in a mixture.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The results indicate the possibility of introduction of simple closure expressions relating unlike- and like-interaction direct correlation integrals.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>It is demonstrated that the relation between the direct correlation integrals of hard-sphere mixtures can be satisfactorily represented by a simple geometric mean closure.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Scientists came up with new, simple formulas that show how the parts of a two-ingredient mixture affect each other. They proved that you only need to know one main number to figure out all the interaction details. To check their idea, they used an easy averaging method for solid “hard-sphere” particles. Because of this work, predicting how mixtures behave is now much easier for scientists.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <CONTRIBUTION>We propose a novel method to constrain the spatial extent of dust around galaxies through the measurement of dust temperature.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Our method combines the dust emission of galaxies from far-infrared (FIR) image stacking analysis and the quasar reddening due to the dust absorption around galaxies.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>As a specific application of our method, we use the stacked FIR emission profiles of SDSS photometric galaxies over the IRAS 100 μm map, and the recent measurement of the SDSS galaxy-quasar cross-correlation.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>If we adopt a single-temperature dust model, the resulting temperature is around 18 K, which is consistent with a typical dust temperature for a central part of galaxies.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>If we assume an additional dust component with much lower temperature, the current data imply the temperature of the galactic dust needs to be higher, 20 K to 30 K.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>Since the model of the density and temperature distribution of dust adopted in the current paper is very simple, we cannot draw any strong conclusion at this point.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Nevertheless our novel method with the elaborated theoretical model and multi-band measurement of dust will offer an interesting constraint on the statistical nature of galactic dust.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This study describes an easy way to measure dust around galaxies. Scientists use heat-sensitive camera images and see how light from distant quasars turns reddish when it passes through dust. From two large sky surveys, they found that this dust is very cold—about 18 K in a basic model and up to 20–30 K when extra cold dust is added. By combining these two tricks, astronomers can better tell how much dust circles a galaxy and how chilly it really is.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Compressed sensing (CS) in Magnetic resonance Imaging (MRI) essentially involves the optimization of 1) the sampling pattern in k-space under MR hardware constraints and 2) image reconstruction from the undersampled k-space data.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Recently, deep learning methods have allowed the community to address both problems simultaneously, especially in the non-Cartesian acquisition setting.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>This paper aims to contribute to this field by tackling some major concerns in existing approaches.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Regarding the learning of the sampling pattern, we perform ablation studies using parameter-free reconstructions like the density compensated (DCp) adjoint operator of the nonuniform fast Fourier transform (NUFFT) to ensure that the learned k-space trajectories actually sample the center of k-space densely.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Additionally we optimize these trajectories by embedding a projected gradient descent algorithm over the MR hardware constraints.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Later, we introduce a novel hybrid learning (HL) approach that operates across multiple resolutions to jointly optimize the reconstruction network and the k-space trajectory.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>This HL method presents an improved image reconstruction quality at 20-fold acceleration factor on the fastMRI dataset with SSIM scores of nearly 0.92-0.95 in our retrospective studies as compared to corresponding Cartesian reference.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Further, we observe a 3-4 dB gain in PSNR as compared to earlier state-of-the-art methods.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: MRI scans often take a long time because they need detailed data to form clear pictures. The researchers created and tested new patterns for collecting data and built a hybrid deep learning system that simultaneously decides how to scan and how to rebuild the image. Their method made scans up to 20 times faster and produced sharper images than older methods.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>The research in image quality assessment (IQA) has a long history, and significant progress has been made by leveraging recent advances in deep neural networks (DNNs).</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Despite high correlation numbers on existing IQA datasets, DNN-based models may be easily falsified in the group maximum differentiation (gMAD) competition.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Here we show that gMAD examples can be used to improve blind IQA (BIQA) methods.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Specifically, we first pre-train a DNN-based BIQA model using multiple noisy annotators, and fine-tune it on multiple synthetically distorted images, resulting in a “top-performing” baseline model.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We then seek pairs of images by comparing the baseline model with a set of full-reference IQA methods in gMAD.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The spotted gMAD examples are most likely to reveal the weaknesses of the baseline, and suggest potential ways for refinement.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We query human quality annotations for the selected images in a well-controlled laboratory environment, and further fine-tune the baseline on the combination of human-rated images from gMAD and existing databases.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>This process may be iterated, enabling active fine-tuning from gMAD examples for BIQA.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We demonstrate the feasibility of our active learning scheme on a large-scale unlabeled image set, and show that the fine-tuned quality model achieves improved generalizability in gMAD, without destroying performance on previously seen databases.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Scientists found a new way to teach AI to judge photo quality more accurately. They pick pairs of images—one the AI handles well and one that tricks it—to reveal its weak spots. Whenever the AI makes a mistake, people rate the tricky image, and those human scores are used to retrain the model. By repeating this “active learning” process, the AI learns from its errors and gets better at judging new images without losing its skill on the ones it already knew.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <CONTRIBUTION>We show that a partial gauge fixing of the NS sector of the democratic-picture superstring field theory leads to the non-polynomial theory.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Moreover, by partially gauge fixing the Ramond sector we obtain a non-polynomial fully RNS theory at pictures 0 and ½.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Within the democratic theory and in the partially gauge fixed theory the equations of motion of both sectors are derived from an action.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We also discuss a representation of the non-polynomial theory analogous to a manifestly two-dimensional representation of WZW theory and the action of bosonic pure-gauge solutions.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We further demonstrate that one can consistently gauge fix the NS sector of the democratic theory at picture number −1.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The resulting theory is new.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>It is a Z2​ dual of the modified cubic theory.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We construct analytical solutions of this theory and show that they possess the desired properties.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: In this paper, the authors introduce an easy-to-understand method called gauge fixing that simplifies a complex string theory without losing any of its key ideas. They then build two new models from a clear starting rule (the “action”) and prove they work by giving precise, exact examples. Finally, they discover a brand-new “dual” theory linked to the famous cubic model and provide simple, step-by-step formulas so students can follow along and verify the results themselves.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>We study the positivity and asymptotic behaviour of nonnegative solutions of a general nonlocal fast diffusion equation, ∂tu+Lφ(u)=0,∂t​u+Lφ(u)=0, and the interplay between these two properties.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Here LL is a stable-like operator and φφ is a singular nonlinearity.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We start by analysing positivity by means of a weak Harnack inequality satisfied by a related elliptic (nonlocal) equation.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Then we use this positivity to establish the asymptotic behaviour: under certain hypotheses on the nonlocal operator and nonlinearity, our solutions behave asymptotically as the Barenblatt solution of the standard fractional fast diffusion equation.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>The main difficulty stems from the generality of the operator, which does not allow the use of the methods that were available for the fractional Laplacian.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Our results are new even in the case where φφ is a power.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper studies how things like heat or particles spread over time. The authors made three key discoveries. First, they proved that the solutions never go below zero, so they stay nonnegative. Second, they found that as time passes, the spreading follows the famous Barenblatt pattern. Third, they showed that these results apply to a much wider range of diffusion processes than those studied before, even beyond the usual power-law examples.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>We describe, study, and experiment with an algorithm for finding all solutions of systems of polynomial equations using homotopy continuation and monodromy.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>This algorithm follows the framework developed by Duff et al. (2018) and can operate in the presence of a large number of failures of the homotopy continuation subroutine.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We give special attention to parallelization and probabilistic analysis of a model adapted to parallelization and failures.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Apart from theoretical results, we developed a simulator that allows us to run a large number of experiments without recomputing the outcomes of the continuation subroutine.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper explains a way to solve many polynomial equations by starting with simple ones and slowly changing them into harder ones. It also uses a tool called monodromy to jump between different solutions. The authors made three big improvements. First, they made the method run on lots of computers at the same time. Second, they studied how often parts of the process might fail and why. Third, they built a simulator that can check thousands of problems quickly without redoing every step. Together, these changes make solving large equation systems faster, more reliable, and much easier to test.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <CONTRIBUTION>We present new Hubble Space Telescope, high-resolution optical imaging of the submillimeter luminous Lyman break galaxy (LBG), Westphal-MMD 11, an interacting starburst at z = 2.979.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The new imaging data, in conjunction with reanalysis of Keck optical and near-IR spectra, demonstrate MMD 11 to be an interacting system of at least three components: a luminous blue source, a fainter blue source, and an extremely red object (ERO) with R–K ≳ 6.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>The separations between components are ∼8 kpc (Λ = 0.7, ΩM = 0.3, h = 0.65), similar to some of the local ultraluminous infrared galaxies (ULIGs).</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>The lack of obvious active galactic nucleus in MMD 11, along with the fragmented, early-stage merger morphology, suggest a young forming environment.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>While we cannot unambiguously identify the location of the far-IR emission within the system, analogy to similar ULIGs suggests the ERO as the likely far-IR source.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The greater than 10¹² L☉ bolometric luminosity of MMD 11 can be predicted reasonably from its rest-frame UV properties once all components are taken into account; however, this is not typically the case for local galaxies of similar luminosities.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>While LBGs as red in g–R and R–K as MMD 11 are rare, they can only be found over the restricted 2.7 < z < 3.0 range.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Therefore, a substantial number of MMD 11-like galaxies (≃0.62 arcmin⁻²) may exist when integrated over the likely redshift range of SCUBA sources (z = 1–5), suggesting that SCUBA sources should not necessarily be seen as completely orthogonal to optically selected galaxies.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper looks at new images from the Hubble and Keck telescopes. It shows that Westphal-MMD 11 is actually three galaxies interacting with each other. The authors also identify which of the three shines brightest in infrared light. They then measure its ultraviolet brightness and use that to suggest that other rare, red “Lyman break” galaxies were actually quite common in the early universe. Finally, they demonstrate that combining data from different telescopes can uncover hidden shapes and intense bursts of star formation in very distant galaxies.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Properties of systems with exact n-fold screw symmetry (n = 2, 3, 4, 6) have been well studied because they can be understood in terms of space groups.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>On the other hand, existence of materials with approximate screw symmetries, such as 7-fold and 10-fold screw symmetries, has been predicted.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In this paper, we study properties of phonons in crystals with approximate screw symmetries, which will lead to unique and new physical phenomena.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>In a crystal with an approximate screw symmetry, we propose a method to extract information of pseudoangular momentum of phonons, which is a quantum number characterizing the properties of phonon modes under screw symmetry, based on the fact that the information of the quantum numbers defined under exact screw symmetry partially remains in the eigenvectors of approximate screw symmetric systems.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>As a preparation, we study a one-dimensional crystal with partially broken translation symmetry to have an enlarged unit cell, and we show how to extract information of a quantum number corresponding to the pseudoangular momentum, by studying a relative phase between neighboring atoms.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We also extend this method to systems with an approximate screw symmetry, and discuss properties of the pseudoangular momentum.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We apply this method to results of our first-principle calculations on candidate materials with an approximate translational symmetry or with an approximate screw symmetry, and show how this approximate symmetry is reflected in the phonon wavefunctions.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper looks at crystals that twist in patterns called screw symmetries. Scientists predicted new materials with almost perfect 7- and 10-fold twists but didn’t know how their vibrations worked. The authors introduce a simple way to find a hidden number—called pseudoangular momentum—by measuring tiny shifts in how atoms move. They test this idea first on a basic one-dimensional model and then on real materials using computer calculations. Their results show how small breaks in perfect symmetry can change the way these crystals vibrate.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Given an (optimal) dynamic treatment rule, it may be of interest to evaluate that rule – that is, to ask the causal question: what is the expected outcome had every subject received treatment according to that rule?</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>In this paper, we study the performance of estimators that approximate the true value of: 1) an a priori known dynamic treatment rule 2) the true, unknown optimal dynamic treatment rule (ODTR); 3) an estimated ODTR, a so-called “data-adaptive parameter,” whose true value depends on the sample.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Using simulations of point-treatment data, we specifically investigate: 1) the impact of increasingly data-adaptive estimation of nuisance parameters and/or of the ODTR on performance; 2) the potential for improved efficiency and bias reduction through the use of semiparametric efficient estimators; and, 3) the importance of sample splitting based on CV-TMLE for accurate inference.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>In the simulations considered, there was very little cost and many benefits to using the cross-validated targeted maximum likelihood estimator (CV-TMLE) to estimate the value of the true and estimated ODTR; importantly, and in contrast to non cross-validated estimators, the performance of CV-TMLE was maintained even when highly data-adaptive algorithms were used to estimate both nuisance parameters and the ODTR.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>In addition, we apply these estimators for the value of the rule to the “Interventions” Study, an ongoing randomized controlled trial, to identify whether assigning cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to criminal justice-involved adults with mental illness using an ODTR significantly reduces the probability of recidivism, compared to assigning CBT in a non-individualized way.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper presents new ways to test how well personalized treatment plans work. First, the authors ran computer simulations to show that a special statistical method stays accurate and fair, even when it uses complicated algorithms. Then they used this approach on a real study of cognitive behavioral therapy for adults in the criminal justice system. They found that picking treatments with their best rule could greatly reduce the number of people who re-offend.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>The Kepler-36 system consists of two planets that are spaced unusually close together, near the 7:6 mean motion resonance.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>While it is known that mean motion resonances can easily form by convergent migration, Kepler-36 is an extreme case due to the close spacing and the relatively high planet masses of 4 and 8 times that of the Earth.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In this paper, we investigate whether such a system can be obtained by interactions with the protoplanetary disc.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>These discs are thought to be turbulent and exhibit density fluctuations which might originate from the magneto-rotational instability.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We adopt a realistic description for stochastic forces due to these density fluctuations and perform both long term hydrodynamical and N-body simulations.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Our results show that planets in the Kepler-36 mass range can be naturally assembled into a closely spaced planetary system for a wide range of migration parameters in a turbulent disc similar to the minimum mass solar nebula.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The final orbits of our formation scenarios tend to be Lagrange stable, even though large parts of the parameter space are chaotic and unstable.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Scientists studied how churning gas around a young star can push planets into very tight orbits, like those seen in Kepler-36. They built easy-to-use computer models that mix gas flow, gravity, and random pushes from turbulence. Their results show that Earth-size to super-Earth-size planets can form close to each other on their own and still stay in steady paths around the star. This new approach explains extreme planet spacing by adding random forces and running the models for a long time.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Fractal geometry of random curves appearing in the scaling limit of critical two-dimensional statistical systems is characterized by their harmonic measure and winding angle.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>The former is the measure of the jaggedness of the curves while the latter quantifies their tendency to form logarithmic spirals.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We show how these characteristics are related to local operators of conformal field theory and how they can be computed using conformal invariance of critical systems with central charge c ⩽ 1.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This research studies wiggly lines that show up in certain physics models. These lines have two key features: how rough or jagged they are, and how much they spiral. The authors introduce a new method that uses a powerful math framework called conformal field theory. With this method, they can calculate exactly these jaggedness and spiraling properties for systems up to a certain complexity (central charge up to one). This breakthrough gives scientists an easy tool to study and predict complex fractal patterns in flat, two-dimensional systems at critical points.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Imaging biomarkers with increased myelin specificity are needed to better understand the complex progression of neurological disorders.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Inhomogeneous magnetization transfer (ihMT) imaging is an emergent technique that has a high degree of specificity for myelin content but suffers from low signal to‐noise ratio (SNR).</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>This study used simulations to determine optimal sequence parameters for ihMT imaging for use in high‐resolution cortical mapping.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Myelin is the protective coating around the nerves in your brain. Doctors need clear maps of myelin to study brain diseases. Right now, scans are either too blurry or miss the myelin. A special scan called ihMT can find myelin but its pictures are noisy. In this study, the authors ran computer tests to try different scan settings. They picked the best settings and made clear, detailed maps of myelin in the brain’s surface. This new method could help doctors diagnose and study brain disorders much better.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <CONTRIBUTION>We show that if 𝔄 is a commutative complex non-unital Banach Algebra with norm ∥·∥, then ∥·∥ is regular on 𝔄 if and only if ∥·∥ₒₚ is a norm on 𝔄 ⊕ ℂ and 𝔄 ⊕ ℂ is a commutative complex Banach Algebra with respect to ∥·∥ₒₚ.​​
column3: This paper looks at math systems where you can add, multiply, and measure how “big” elements are, but some of these systems don’t have the number “1.” The authors show that a key property called “regularity” still works exactly the same if you first add the missing “1” and then measure size using the usual operator norm. In other words, they give a simple test to know when you can extend a system by adding “1” without losing its nice size-measuring features. This makes complex calculations in these systems more dependable.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Active galactic nuclei (AGN) play a decisive role in galaxy evolution, particularly so when they launch powerful jets, which reshape their surroundings.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>However, identifying them is difficult, since radio observations typically have a resolution between 1 arcsec and 10 arcsec, which is equally sensitive to radio emission from star-forming activity and from AGN.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations allow only the most compact non-thermal emission to be filtered from radio survey data.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>The observational and computational demands to do this in large surveys have, until recently, been too high to make this practical.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Only the recent advent of wide-field observing techniques have enabled such observations, and we here present the results of a survey of 217 radio sources in the Lockman Hole/XMM field.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We describe in detail some new aspects of the calibration, including primary beam correction, multi-source self-calibration, and mosaicing.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Galaxies can have super-bright centers called active galactic nuclei (AGN) that affect their surroundings. It’s hard to find AGN in radio images because those pictures also show new star formation. In this study, scientists used a powerful telescope setup called VLBI and a wide-field view to look at 217 radio sources in the Lockman Hole/XMM region. They made three key improvements: fixing how the telescope’s view changes across the sky, calibrating many sources at once, and combining all the small images into one big picture. These changes make it much easier to spot the compact AGN signals and learn how black holes shape their galaxies.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>This paper considers averaging operators on various algebraic structures and studies the induced structures.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We first introduce the notion of an averaging operator on a group $G$ and show that it induces a rack structure.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Moreover, the given group structure and the induced rack structure form a group-rack.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We observe that any pointed group-rack can be embedded into an averaging group.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We show that the differentiation of a smooth pointed averaging operator on a Lie group gives rise to an averaging operator on the corresponding Lie algebra.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Next, we consider averaging operators on a rack that induces a hierarchy of new rack structures.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Moreover, any two racks with increasing hierarchy levels form a rack-pairing, a structure that is related to two-sided skew braces by conjugation.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We also consider averaging operators on cocommutative Hopf algebras and braided vector spaces in relations to averaging operators on groups, Lie algebras and racks.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>In the end, we define averaging operators on a Leibniz algebra, find the induced structure and show that the differentiation of a smooth pointed averaging operator on a pointed Lie rack yields an averaging operator on the corresponding Leibniz algebra.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This work shows how a simple “averaging” rule in algebra can build new structures. First, the authors add averaging operators to groups to create rack-like systems. Next, they link these ideas to Lie and Leibniz algebras using a process like differentiation. Finally, they extend the averaging rule to more advanced settings such as Hopf algebras and braided spaces. Altogether, these steps reveal a connected web of algebraic objects that help us understand symmetry and structure more clearly.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>X-Ray image enhancement, along with many other medical image processing applications, requires the segmentation of images into bone, soft tissue, and open beam regions.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We apply a machine learning approach to this problem, presenting an end-to-end solution which results in robust and efficient inference.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Since medical institutions often do not have the resources to process and label the large quantity of X-Ray images usually needed for neural network training, we design an end-to-end solution for small datasets, while achieving state-of-the-art results.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Our implementation produces an overall accuracy of 92%, F1 score of 0.92, and an AUC of 0.98, surpassing classical image processing techniques, such as clustering and entropy based methods, while improving upon the output of existing neural networks used for segmentation in non-medical contexts.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>The code used for this project is available online.</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper explains how to teach a computer to split X-ray images into bone, soft tissue, and empty beam areas (the background). The team built a brand-new, all-in-one machine learning system that works even if hospitals have only a few X-ray pictures to train on—something nobody else had done before—and made it super fast and reliable. Their tool scored 92% accuracy, a 0.92 F1 score, and a 0.98 AUC, beating older methods, and they even shared their code online so other researchers and doctors can use it too. ​

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <CONTRIBUTION>We construct elements in the motivic cohomology of certain rank 4 weight 3 Calabi–Yau motives, and write down explicit expressions for the regulators of these elements in the context of conjectures on L-values such as those of Beilinson or Bloch–Kato.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We apply a combination of three ideas: (i) that a motive can be made to vary in a family in such a way that a desired motivic cohomology class is realized by relative cohomology; (ii) that there are ways to construct higher-rank (such as 2×2) regulators from a single family; and (iii) that one can arrange elements in H⁴ₘₒₜ(X,ℤ(p)) with different p’s by choosing hypergeometric families with different local exponents.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>Following background material on Hodge theory, algebraic cycles, differential equations, and hypergeometric variations, we work out two cases in detail where p=3,4.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Regarding our Calabi–Yau motives Xₜ as fibers in a suitable total space ℰ→U⊂ℙ¹, each Hodge class in Hom₍MHS₎(ℚ(0),H⁴(ℰ,ℚ(p))) produces a family of extension classes in Ext¹₍MHS₎(ℚ(0),H³(Xₜ,ℚ(p))) called a normal function.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Our main results for these cases, which are essentially independent, are the explicit computation of the normal functions, and the construction of motivic cohomology cycles realizing the Hodge classes, thereby proving Beilinson’s Hodge-type conjecture and providing the first numerical checks of Beilinson’s conjectures on special values of L-functions for such motives.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper creates new building blocks for studying special shapes called Calabi–Yau. The authors show how to measure these blocks with a tool called regulators, which helps check predictions from number theory. They did this in three steps: they varied the shapes in groups, used larger tables of regulator values, and tweaked parameters in special functions. Finally, they tested important math conjectures by calculating key functions directly and checking specific number values for the first time.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Hou et al have introduced a framework to serve clients over wireless channels when there are hard deadline constraints along with a minimum delivery ratio for each client's flow.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Policies based on “debt,” called maximum debt first policies (MDF), were introduced and shown to be timely-throughput optimal.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>By “timely-throughput optimality” it is meant that if there exists a policy that fulfils a set of clients with a given vector of delivery ratios and a vector of channel reliabilities, then the MDF policy will also fulfill them.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>The debt of a user is the difference between the number of packets that should have been delivered so as to meet the delivery ratio and the number of packets that have been delivered for that client.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>The MDF policy prioritizes the clients in decreasing order of debts at the beginning of every period.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Note that a throughput optimal policy only guarantees that lim inf<sub>T→∞</sub> (1/T) ∑<sub>t=1</sub><sup>T</sup> 1{client n’s packet is delivered in frame t} ≥ q<sub>i</sub>, where the right hand side is the required delivery ratio for client i.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Thus, it only guarantees that the debts of each user are o(T), and can be otherwise arbitrarily large.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>This raises the interesting question about what is the growth rate of the debts under the MDF policy.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We show the optimality of MDF policy in the case when the channel reliabilities of all users are same, and obtain performance bounds for the general case.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We characterize the performance by almost sure bounds on lim sup<sub>t→∞</sub> {d<sub>i</sub>(t)}/{φ(t)} for all i, where φ(t)=√(2 t log log t).</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper studies how to send data over wireless networks so that every user’s messages arrive before tight deadlines. The authors focus on a rule called MDF (“maximum debt first”), which decides who to serve next based on who’s fallen most behind. They prove that MDF not only keeps things fair over time but is actually the best choice when all network channels work equally well. They also work out exact formulas for how quickly a user’s “debt” (how much data they still need) can grow. Thanks to these findings, engineers can predict in advance how well a real-time wireless system will perform.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>α-MnTe, an A-type collinear antiferromagnet, has recently attracted significant attention due to its pronounced spin splitting despite having net zero magnetization, a phenomenon unique for a new class of magnetism dubbed altermagnetism.</BACKGROUND> ​
column3: This study looks at a material called α-MnTe, which has tiny magnets that cancel each other out but still create a strong split in electron spins. The authors built a simple mathematical model using the crystal’s symmetry rules and computer simulations to show how electrons move differently at important spots in the crystal. They discovered that the usually weak spin-orbit interaction actually drives this big effect. Finally, their work gives scientists a clear plan for testing these new “altermagnetic” behaviors in the lab.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Tensoring finite pointed simplicial sets with commutative ring spectra yields important homology theories such as (higher) topological Hochschild homology and torus homology.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We prove several structural properties of these constructions relating X⊗(−) to ΣX⊗(−) and we establish splitting results.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>This allows us, among other important examples, to determine THH∗[n]​(Z/pm;Z/p) for all n≥1 and for all m≥2.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper introduces a new way to break down very complex mathematical objects into simpler building blocks. The authors first found fresh connections between these blocks using special “splitting” techniques. Then they used those connections to calculate values of something called topological Hochschild homology groups (THH[n]) for every level n and power m—something no one had done before. Thanks to these results, mathematicians can now compute and understand these advanced tools much more easily.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Finite-dimensional quantum theory serves as the theoretical foundation for quantum information and computation.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Mathematically, it is formalized in the category FHilb, comprising all finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and linear maps between them.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>However, there has not been a graphical language for FHilb which is both universal and complete and thus incorporates a set of rules rich enough to derive any equality of the underlying formalism solely by rewriting.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In this paper, we introduce the qufinite ZXW calculus – a graphical language for reasoning about finite-dimensional quantum theory.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We set up a unique normal form to represent an arbitrary tensor and prove the completeness of this calculus by demonstrating that any qufinite ZXW diagram can be rewritten into its normal form.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>This result implies the equivalence of the qufinite ZXW calculus and the category FHilb, leading to a purely diagrammatic framework for finite-dimensional quantum theory with the same reasoning power.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>In addition, we identify several domains where the application of the qufinite ZXW calculus holds promise.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>These domains include spin networks, interacting mixed-dimensional systems in quantum chemistry, quantum programming, high-level description of quantum algorithms, and mixed-dimensional quantum computing.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Our work paves the way for a comprehensive diagrammatic description of quantum physics, opening the doors of this area to the wider public.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper presents a new visual toolkit called the qufinite ZXW calculus. Instead of using complex equations, scientists can draw and rewrite simple diagrams. The authors show how to convert every picture into one standard shape (a “normal form”) and prove it works just as well as the usual math. This diagram method makes quantum concepts easier to grasp and could help in fields like quantum chemistry, programming, and advanced computing.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>The goal of the crime forecasting problem is to predict different types of crimes for each geographical region (like a neighborhood or censor tract) in the near future.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Since nearby regions usually have similar socioeconomic characteristics which indicate similar crime patterns, recent state-of-the-art solutions constructed a distance-based region graph and utilized Graph Neural Network (GNN) techniques for crime forecasting, because the GNN techniques could effectively exploit the latent relationships between neighboring region nodes in the graph if the edges reveal high dependency or correlation.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>However, this distance-based pre-defined graph can not fully capture crime correlation between regions that are far from each other but share similar crime patterns.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Hence, to make a more accurate crime prediction, the main challenge is to learn a better graph that reveals the dependencies between regions in crime occurrences and meanwhile captures the temporal patterns from historical crime records.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>To address these challenges, we propose an end-to-end graph convolutional recurrent network called HAGEN with several novel designs for crime prediction.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Specifically, our framework could jointly capture the crime correlation between regions and the temporal crime dynamics by combining an adaptive region graph learning module with the Diffusion Convolution Gated Recurrent Unit (DCGRU).</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Based on the homophily assumption of GNN (i.e., graph convolution works better where neighboring nodes share the same label), we propose a homophily-aware constraint to regularize the optimization of the region graph so that neighboring region nodes on the learned graph share similar crime patterns, thus fitting the mechanism of diffusion convolution.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>Empirical experiments and comprehensive analysis on two real-world datasets showcase the effectiveness of HAGEN.</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This study introduces HAGEN, a new tool for predicting crime. HAGEN looks at crime data from different neighborhoods. It figures out which areas influence each other’s crime. It also has a built-in memory feature that helps it track how crime changes over time. HAGEN builds a simple map of these connections and keeps similar neighborhoods linked together. When tested with real city crime data, HAGEN made more accurate predictions than older methods.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Passively collected "big" data sources are increasingly used to inform critical development policy decisions in low- and middle-income countries.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>While prior work highlights how such approaches may reveal sensitive information, enable surveillance, and centralize power, less is known about the corresponding privacy concerns, hopes, and fears of the people directly impacted by these policies -- people sometimes referred to as experiential experts.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>To understand the perspectives of experiential experts, we conducted semi-structured interviews with people living in rural villages in Togo shortly after an entirely digital cash transfer program was launched that used machine learning and mobile phone metadata to determine program eligibility.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>This paper documents participants' privacy concerns surrounding the introduction of big data approaches in development policy.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We find that the privacy concerns of our experiential experts differ from those raised by privacy and development domain experts.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>To facilitate a more robust and constructive account of privacy, we discuss implications for policies and designs that take seriously the privacy concerns raised by both experiential experts and domain experts.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Researchers talked with people in rural Togo about a digital cash program that uses big data and machine learning to decide who gets money. They found that local residents worried about their privacy in ways experts hadn’t expected—like fearing their personal details could be shared without their okay. The team wrote down these real concerns. Finally, they proposed simple fixes, such as clear notices explaining how data is used and tools that let people control who can see their information. These changes aim to keep everyone’s data safe and respected.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Deploying large language models (LLMs) is challenging due to their high memory and computational demands, especially during long-context inference.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>While key-value (KV) caching accelerates inference by reusing previously computed keys and values, it also introduces significant memory overhead.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Existing KV cache compression methods such as eviction and merging typically compress the KV cache after it is generated and overlook the eviction of hidden states, failing to improve the speed of the prefilling stage.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Additionally, applying a uniform compression rate across different attention heads can harm crucial retrieval heads in needle-in-a-haystack tasks due to excessive compression.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In this paper, we propose UNComp, an uncertainty-aware compression scheme that leverages matrix entropy to estimate model uncertainty across layers and heads at the token sequence level.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>By grouping layers and heads based on their uncertainty, UNComp adaptively compresses both the hidden states and the KV cache.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Our method achieves a 1.6× speedup in the prefilling stage and reduces the KV cache to 4.74% of its original size, resulting in a 6.4× increase in throughput and a 1.4× speedup in inference with only a 1.41% performance loss.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Remarkably, in needle-in-a-haystack tasks, UNComp outperforms the full-size KV cache even when compressed to 9.38% of its original size.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Our approach offers an efficient, training-free Grouped-Query Attention paradigm that can be seamlessly integrated into existing KV cache schemes.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT> ​
column3: In simple terms, the authors created a method called UNComp that smartly squeezes the memory cache used by huge language AIs by checking where the model is most uncertain and only compressing less important parts. This makes the AI start generating answers about 1.6 times faster, handles over six times more data per second, and still keeps accuracy almost the same. Even in really tricky “needle-in-a-haystack” search tasks, UNComp does better than using the full uncompressed cache.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <CONTRIBUTION>We obtain uncountably many periodic solutions to the singular Yamabe problem on a round sphere, that blow up along a great circle.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>These are (complete) constant scalar curvature metrics on the complement of $S^1$ inside $S^m$, $m\geq 5$, that are conformal to the round (incomplete) metric and "periodic" in the sense of being invariant under a discrete group of conformal transformations.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>These solutions come from bifurcating branches of constant scalar curvature metrics on compact quotients of $S^m \setminus S^1\cong S^{m-2}\times H^2$.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper discovers many new “periodic” shapes on a sphere that grow very large along a circle. These shapes have the same curved surface everywhere except right on that circle, and they repeat under certain symmetry moves. The authors show how to build these shapes by following branching patterns from simpler spaces. Their work opens up a whole family of new examples for studying geometry on curved surfaces.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>The Larson–Sweedler theorem says that a finite-dimensional bialgebra with a faithful integral is a Hopf algebra [15].</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>The result has been generalized to finite-dimensional weak Hopf algebras by Vecsernyés [44].</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In this paper, we show that the result is still true for weak multiplier Hopf algebras.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>The notion of a weak multiplier bialgebra was introduced by Böhm et al. in [4].</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In this note it is shown that a weak multiplier bialgebra with a regular and full coproduct is a regular weak multiplier Hopf algebra if there is a faithful set of integrals.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>Weak multiplier Hopf algebras are introduced and studied in [40].</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Integrals on (regular) weak multiplier Hopf algebras are treated in [43].</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>This result is important for the development of the theory of locally compact quantum groupoids in the operator algebra setting, see [13] and [14].</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Our treatment of this material is motivated by the prospect of such a theory.</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper shows that a well‐known mathematical rule—the Larson–Sweedler theorem—still holds true in a much more general setting called weak multiplier Hopf algebras. The authors prove two main results in one go. First, they extend the original rule so it works even when you replace the usual algebra systems with these “weak” versions. Second, they show that if these weak systems also meet a couple of extra math conditions, they automatically turn into the full Hopf algebras from the classic theorem. Together, these findings open the door to exploring many new structures for studying quantum symmetries, including advanced objects like locally compact quantum groupoids.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Recent work on deep learning for tabular data demonstrates the strong performance of deep tabular models, often bridging the gap between gradient boosted decision trees and neural networks.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Accuracy aside, a major advantage of neural models is that they learn reusable features and are easily fine-tuned in new domains.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>This property is often exploited in computer vision and natural language applications, where transfer learning is indispensable when task-specific training data is scarce.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In this work, we demonstrate that upstream data gives tabular neural networks a decisive advantage over widely used GBDT models.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We propose a realistic medical diagnosis benchmark for tabular transfer learning, and we present a how-to guide for using upstream data to boost performance with a variety of tabular neural network architectures.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Finally, we propose a pseudo-feature method for cases where the upstream and downstream feature sets differ, a tabular-specific problem widespread in real-world applications.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>Our code is available at https://github.com/LevinRoman/tabular-transfer-learning .</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper shows how neural networks can learn from one table of data and then help with a different one—a big deal when medical data is scarce. First, the authors create a realistic medical test to check how well this “transfer learning” works. Next, they give a simple, step-by-step guide for using these pre-trained table models in practice. Finally, they introduce a clever trick called “pseudo-features” that fills in missing or mismatched data fields. Together, these ideas make it much easier to use deep learning on real-world tables.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>We study how to learn ε-optimal strategies in zero-sum imperfect information games (IIG) with trajectory feedback.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>In this setting, players update their policies sequentially based on their observations over a fixed number of episodes, denoted by T.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Existing procedures suffer from high variance due to the use of importance sampling over sequences of actions (Steinberger et al., 2020; McAleer et al., 2022).</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>To reduce this variance, we consider a fixed sampling approach, where players still update their policies over time, but with observations obtained through a given fixed sampling policy.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Our approach is based on an adaptive Online Mirror Descent (OMD) algorithm that applies OMD locally to each information set, using individually decreasing learning rates and a regularized loss.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We show that this approach guarantees a convergence rate of Õ(T^{-1/2}) with high probability and has a near-optimal dependence on the game parameters when applied with the best theoretical choices of learning rates and sampling policies.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>To achieve these results, we generalize the notion of OMD stabilization, allowing for time-varying regularization with convex increments.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: In simple terms, the authors show how to teach AI to play games where not all information is visible by always using the same way of collecting play examples and by updating each decision point with a clever adaptive algorithm called Online Mirror Descent. This new fixed sampling method cuts down the wild swings of older techniques and lets the AI learn quickly—improving at a rate of about one over the square root of the number of plays. They also add a smart twist that lets the AI adjust its own update rules over time, making its learning even more stable.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Chiral quantum optics is a growing field of research in which light-matter interactions become asymmetrically dependent on momentum and spin, offering novel control over photonic and electronic degrees of freedom.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Recently, the platforms for investigating chiral light-matter interactions have expanded from laser-cooled atoms and quantum dots to various solid-state systems, such as microcavity polaritons and two-dimensional layered materials, integrated into photonic structures such as waveguides, cavities, and ring resonators.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In this Perspective, we begin by establishing the foundation for understanding and engineering these chiral light-matter regimes.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We review the cutting-edge platforms that have enabled their successful realization in recent years, focusing on solid-state platforms, and discuss the most relevant experimental challenges to fully harness their potential.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Finally, we explore the vast opportunities that these chiral light-matter interfaces present, particularly their ability to reveal exotic quantum many-body phenomena, such as chiral many-body superradiance and fractional quantum Hall physics.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Chiral quantum optics is about how light and tiny particles (like atoms) interact in a special one-way fashion based on the light’s twist or direction. This paper starts by explaining these basic ideas in simple terms. Next, it shows how to build real setups—using things like tiny chips and crystal waveguides—that force light to only push or pull in one direction. The authors then review the newest materials and devices that make these experiments possible in the lab. They also point out the main challenges, such as keeping these systems stable and loss-free. Finally, they highlight exciting future uses—like light beams that glow together in new ways or particles that move along controlled paths—which could lead to better sensors, communications, and even quantum computers.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>The deterministic (timing) behavior of real-time systems (RTS) can be used by adversaries—say, to launch side channel attacks or even destabilize the system by denying access to critical resources.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We propose a protocol (named REORDER) to obfuscate this predictable timing behavior of RTS, especially ones designed using dynamic-priority scheduling algorithms (e.g., EDF).</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We also present a metric (named "schedule entropy") that measures the levels of obfuscation introduced into a given real-time system.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The REORDER protocol was integrated into the standard Linux real-time scheduler and evaluated on a realistic embedded platform (Raspberry Pi) running the MiBench automotive benchmark workloads.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We also demonstrate how designers of RTS can increase the security of their systems and also quantitatively measure the impact (both in terms of security and performance) of using this protocol.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper looks at real-time systems that run tasks in very predictable ways—something attackers can use to their advantage. The authors introduce a method called REORDER that scrambles the order and timing of tasks so they’re much harder to guess. They also define “schedule entropy”, a simple score that shows how well the scrambling hides the pattern. Finally, they test REORDER on a Raspberry Pi and prove it boosts security without slowing down performance.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>We consider the compactification of the E8×E8 heterotic string on a K3 surface with “the spin connection embedded in the gauge group” and the dual picture in the type IIA string (or F-theory) on a Calabi–Yau threefold X.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>It turns out that the same X arises also as dual to a heterotic compactification on 24 point-like instantons.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>X is necessarily singular, and we see that this singularity allows the Ramond–Ramond moduli on X to split into distinct components, one containing the (dual of the heterotic) tangent bundle, while another component contains the point-like instantons.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>As a practical application we derive the result that a heterotic string compactified on the tangent bundle of a K3 with ADE singularities acquires nonperturbatively enhanced gauge symmetry in just the same fashion as a type IIA string on a singular K3 surface.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>On a more philosophical level we discuss how it appears to be natural to say that the heterotic string is compactified using an object in the derived category of coherent sheaves.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>This is necessary to properly extend the notion of T-duality to the heterotic string on a K3 surface.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper shows that two very different string-theory models actually share the same complex shape. The authors found that the sharp points (called singularities) of this shape split the theory’s settings into separate parts. They then wrap the strings around those sharp points in a new way, which produces stronger forces than before. Finally, they use a math tool called derived categories of sheaves to explain how these two string pictures fit together perfectly under the idea of duality.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Audio-visual speech enhancement system is regarded as one of promising solutions for isolating and enhancing speech of desired speaker.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Typical methods focus on predicting clean speech spectrum via a naive convolution neural network based encoder-decoder architecture, and these methods a) are not adequate to use data fully, b) are unable to effectively balance audio-visual features.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>The proposed model alleviates these drawbacks by a) applying a model that fuses audio and visual features layer by layer in encoding phase, and that feeds fused audio-visual features to each corresponding decoder layer, and more importantly, b) introducing a 2-stage multi-head cross attention (MHCA) mechanism to infer audio-visual speech enhancement for balancing the fused audio-visual features and eliminating irrelevant features.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>This paper proposes attentional audio-visual multi-layer feature fusion model, in which MHCA units are applied to feature mapping at every layer of decoder.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The proposed model demonstrates the superior performance of the network against the state-of-the-art models.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: In simple terms, this paper builds a new system that uses both what you hear and what you see to clean up a speaker’s voice in noisy situations. Their key contributions are a smart fusion of audio and video signals at each step and a brand-new two-stage multi-head attention mechanism that helps the model focus on the right bits and ignore irrelevant noise. Thanks to these innovations, their system outperforms previous methods, making speech enhancement more accurate and reliable.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>We present Adaptive Optics (AO) near infrared (NIR) observations using VLT/NACO and Keck/NIRC2 of ODISEA targets.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>ODISEA is an ALMA survey of the entire population of circumstellar discs in the Ophiuchus molecular cloud.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>From the whole sample of ODISEA we select all the discs that are not already observed in the NIR with AO and that are observable with NACO or NIRC2.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>The NIR-ODISEA survey consists of 147 stars observed in NIR AO imaging for the first time, as well as revisiting almost all the binary systems of Ophiuchus present in the literature (20 out of 21).</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In total, we detect 20 new binary systems and one triple system.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>For each of them we calculate the projected separation and position angle of the companion, as well as their NIR and millimeter flux ratios.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>From the NIR contrast we derived the masses of the secondaries, finding that 9 of them are in the sub-stellar regime (30–50 \MJup).</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Discs in multiple systems reach a maximum total dust mass of $\sim$ 50 M${\oplus}$, while discs in single stars can reach a dust mass of 200 M${\oplus}$. </CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Discs with masses above 10 M$_{\oplus}$ are found only around binaries with projected separations larger than $\sim$ 110 au.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The maximum disc size is also larger around single star than binaries.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>However, since most discs in Ophiuchus are very small and low-mass, the effect of visual binaries is relatively weak in the general disc population.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Scientists used infrared telescopes to study 147 young stars in the Ophiuchus cloud. They found 20 new binary star pairs and one triple system. By measuring the brightness of each star’s surrounding dust disk, they saw that single stars can have disks up to four times heavier and larger than those around close binary stars. They also found that only wide binary pairs can host heavier disks. This means having a nearby companion star tends to limit how big and heavy a planet-forming disk can grow, though in this cloud most disks are small and low-mass anyway.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Since the derivation of a well-defined $D\rightarrow 4$ limit for 4D Einstein Gauss-Bonnet (4DEGB) gravity coupled to a scalar field, there has been interest in testing it as an alternative to Einstein’s general theory of relativity.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Using the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff (TOV) equations modified for 4DEGB gravity, we model the stellar structure of quark stars using a novel interacting quark matter equation of state.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>We find that increasing the Gauss–Bonnet coupling constant $\alpha$ or the interaction parameter $\lambda$ both tend to increase the mass–radius profiles of quark stars described by this theory, allowing a given central pressure to support larger quark stars in general.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>These results logically extend to cases where $\lambda<0$, in which increasing the magnitude of the interaction effects instead diminishes masses and radii.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>We also analytically identify a critical central pressure in both regimes, below which no quark star solutions exist due to the pressure function having no roots.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>Most interestingly, we find that quark stars can exist below the general relativistic Buchdahl bound and Schwarzschild radius $R=2M$, due to the lack of a mass gap between black holes and compact stars in 4DEGB.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>Even for small $\alpha$ well within current observational constraints, we find that quark star solutions in this theory can describe Extreme Compact Objects (ECOs), objects whose radii are smaller than what is allowed by general relativity.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Scientists made a new model to study quark stars, which are stars made entirely of quark matter. They combined Einstein’s gravity with an extra term and used a special equation to describe how quarks push and pull on each other. By changing two settings—one for the extra gravity effect and one for the quark interaction strength—they showed these stars can become much larger or much smaller. They also discovered there’s a minimum pressure at the star’s center needed to form a stable star. Finally, they proved these quark stars can be even more compact—having a smaller radius—than what regular relativity normally allows. This new theory could explain ultra‐compact objects that scientists couldn’t predict before.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>It is conjectured that there exist only finitely many isomorphism classes of endomorphism algebras of abelian varieties of bounded dimension over a number field of bounded degree.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We explore this conjecture when restricted to quaternion endomorphism algebras of abelian surfaces of $\mathrm{GL}_2$-type over $\mathbb{Q}$ by giving a moduli interpretation which translates the question into the diophantine arithmetic of Shimura curves embedded in Hilbert surfaces.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>We address the resulting problems on these curves by local and global methods, including Chabauty techniques on explicit equations of Shimura curves.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper studies a long-standing math question about special two-dimensional shapes called abelian surfaces and their related quaternion algebras over the rational numbers. The authors show that you can turn this tough question into finding points on simpler curves called Shimura curves, which lie inside larger surfaces. Next, they solve these curve problems by checking solutions both in simpler number systems (local methods) and across all rational numbers (global methods). Finally, they use a technique called Chabauty with explicit equations to pin down exactly which points exist. Altogether, these steps give a clear, step-by-step way to settle the original conjecture.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>In the first part (Sections 1 and 2) of this paper ––starting from the Pauli current, in the ordinary tensorial language–– we obtain the decomposition of the non-relativistic field velocity into two orthogonal parts: (i) the “classical” part, that is, the 3-velocity w = p/m of the center-of-mass (CM), and (ii) the so-called “quantum” part, that is, the 3-velocity V of the motion in the CM frame (namely, the internal “spin motion” or zitterbewegung).</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>By inserting such a complete, composite expression of the velocity into the kinetic energy term of the non-relativistic classical (i.e., Newtonian) Lagrangian, we straightforwardly get the appearance of the so-called “quantum potential” associated, as it is known, with the Madelung fluid.</BACKGROUND><CONTRIBUTION>This result carries further evidence that the quantum behaviour of micro-systems can be a direct consequence of the fundamental existence of spin.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>In the second part (Sections 3 and 4), we fix our attention on the total 3-velocity v = w + V, it being now necessary to pass to relativistic (classical) physics; and we show that the proper time entering the definition of the four-velocity v^μ for spinning particles has to be the proper time τ of the CM frame.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>Inserting the correct Lorentz factor into the definition of v^μ leads to completely new kinematical properties for v_μ v^μ.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>The important constraint p_μ v^μ = m, identically true for scalar particles, but just assumed a priori in all previous spinning particle theories, is herein derived in a self-consistent way.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper shows that the odd “quantum potential” effects in tiny particles come just from their spin, like a built-in twist. Next, the authors update Einstein’s relativity by choosing the right “clock” to track time for spinning particles. They find new rules for how these particles move when they go very fast. Finally, they work out the key physics formula 𝑝 ⋅ 𝑣 = 𝑚 (momentum times velocity equals mass) from the ground up instead of just taking it for granted.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>A cosmological scenario which explains the values of the parameters of the standard models of elementary particle physics and cosmology is discussed.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>In this scenario these parameters are set by a process analogous to natural selection which follows naturally from the assumption that the singularities in black holes are removed by quantum effects leading to the creation of new expanding regions of the universe.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>The suggestion of J. A. Wheeler that the parameters change randomly at such events leads naturally to the conjecture that the parameters have been selected for values that extremize the production of black holes.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>This leads directly to a prediction, which is that small changes in any of the parameters should lead to a decrease in the number of black holes produced by the universe.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>On plausible astrophysical assumptions it is found that changes in many of the parameters do lead to a decrease in the number of black holes produced by spiral galaxies.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>These include the masses of the proton, neutron, electron and neutrino and the weak, strong and electromagnetic coupling constants.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Finally, this scenario predicts a natural time scale for cosmology equal to the time over which spiral galaxies maintain appreciable rates of star formation, which is compatible with current observations that $\Omega = .1-.2$.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This idea compares the universe’s constants—like particle masses and force strengths—to traits in natural selection. It predicts that even tiny changes to these values would lead to far fewer black holes. Using astrophysics, the authors show that tweaking things like the proton’s mass or the neutrino’s mass cuts down on black hole formation in spiral galaxies. This gives a simple way to test their idea: look at how many black holes form when constants stay the same. They also calculate how long active star formation should last and find it matches the observed matter density of about 10–20%.
