All of these points line up, making their “cosmic natural selection” scenario fit what we actually see in the universe.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>The common spatial pattern analysis (CSP) is a widely used signal processing technique in brain-computer interface (BCI) systems to increase the signal-to-noise ratio in electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Despite its popularity, the CSP's performance is often hindered by the nonstationarity and artifacts in EEG signals.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>The minmax CSP improves the robustness of the CSP by using data-driven covariance matrices to accommodate the uncertainties.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We show that by utilizing the optimality conditions, the minmax CSP can be recast as an eigenvector-dependent nonlinear eigenvalue problem (NEPv).</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We introduce a self-consistent field (SCF) iteration with line search that solves the NEPv of the minmax CSP.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Local quadratic convergence of the SCF for solving the NEPv is illustrated using synthetic datasets.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>More importantly, experiments with real-world EEG datasets show the improved motor imagery classification rates and shorter running time of the proposed SCF-based solver compared to the existing algorithm for the minmax CSP.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper looks at a way to read brain signals using EEG. The authors turned a complex signal-processing method into a simple math problem. Then they designed a fast algorithm to solve it and proved it always finds the right answer quickly. In tests with real brainwave recordings, their solver could tell what movement a person was imagining more accurately and faster than older methods. These improvements make brain-computer interfaces—systems that let you control devices with your thoughts—much more reliable and efficient.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Much of the exoplanet discovery efforts over the next several years are largely tasked with finding candidates for the upcoming Ariel mission.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>This is a role that TESS is well-suited for.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Radial velocity follow-up is needed to confirm the planetary nature of these systems, as many of its planet candidates turn out to be eclipsing binary systems with small stellar secondaries.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Focused Doppler follow-up to obtain these radial velocities is expensive.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>The Gaia mission's radial velocity measurements on its target stars are not adequately precise for a general search for orbiting planetary companions.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>While the RV data has yielded thousands of spectroscopic binary systems, only an extreme minority of these reach into the planetary-mass regime.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Nonetheless, they do detect eclipsing binary systems that can masquerade as transiting hot Jupiters.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In this work, we compare the Gaia DR3 Non-Single Stars catalogue to the current planet candidate list from TESS and determine several of these candidate planetary systems are actually eclipsing binaries.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We find $\sim130$ eclipsing binaries among the TOI and EPIC lists that do not appear to be in the literature, including the previously statistically validated planet K2-256 b.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>This work illustrates the usefulness of \textit{Gaia} to exoplanet validation efforts and will help guide follow-up efforts for discovering new transiting planets for the Ariel mission by avoiding misdirecting valuable telescope time.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper shows how astronomers matched planet candidates from NASA’s TESS telescope with ESA’s Gaia data on stars. They found about 130 “planets” are actually two stars eclipsing each other, not real planets. One of these false alarms was K2-256 b, which people had already thought was a planet. By checking Gaia’s catalog first, scientists can save telescope time and focus on genuine planets—especially those planned for the upcoming Ariel mission.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND> Simulation is the key to scaling up validation and verification for robotic systems such as autonomous vehicles.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND> Despite advances in high-fidelity physics and sensor simulation, a critical gap remains in simulating realistic behaviors of road users.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND> This is because devising first principle models for human-like behaviors is generally infeasible.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION> In this work, we take a data-driven approach to generate traffic behaviors from real-world driving logs.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION> The method achieves high sample efficiency and behavior diversity by exploiting the bi-level hierarchy of high-level intent inference and low-level driving behavior imitation.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION> The method also incorporates a planning module to obtain stable long-horizon behaviors.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION> We empirically validate our method with scenarios from two large-scale driving datasets and show our method achieves balanced traffic simulation performance in realism, diversity, and long-horizon stability.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION> We also explore ways to evaluate behavior realism and introduce a suite of evaluation metrics for traffic simulation.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION> Finally, as part of our core contributions, we develop and open source a software tool that unifies data formats across different driving datasets and converts scenes from existing datasets into interactive simulation environments.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND> For video results and code release, see https://bit.ly/3L9uzj3.</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Most traffic simulators use made-up rules that don’t match how people really drive. This paper introduces a new system that learns directly from real driving data. First, it figures out each driver’s next move, like turning or changing lanes. Then it copies how people drive and adds a simple planning step so cars move smoothly over time. The authors created tests to check that this fake traffic looks realistic and has plenty of variety. They also released a free tool that turns any driving data into a hands-on traffic simulation anyone can try.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>We study the relation between the metallicity of quasar broad line region (BLR) and black hole (BH) mass ($10^{7.5}M_{\odot} \sim 10^{10}M_{\odot}$) and quasar bolometric luminosity ($10^{44.6}erg/s \sim 10^{48} erg/s$) using a sample of $\sim$130,000 quasars at $2.25\leq z\leq 5.25$ from Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Data Release 12 (DR12).</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>We generate composite spectra by stacking individual spectra in the same BH mass (bolometric luminosity) and redshift bins and then estimate the metallicity of quasar BLR using metallicity-sensitive broad emission-line flux ratios based on the photoionization models.</BACKGROUND><CONTRIBUTION>We find a significant correlation between quasar BLR metallicity and BH mass (bolometric luminosity) but no correlation between quasar BLR metallicity and redshift.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>We also compare the metallicity of quasar BLR and that of host galaxies inferred from the mass-metallicity relation of star-forming galaxy at $z\sim2.3$ and $z\sim3.5$.</BACKGROUND><CONTRIBUTION>We find quasar BLR metallicity is 0.3 $\sim$ 1.0 dex higher than their host galaxies.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>This discrepancy cannot be interpreted by the uncertainty due to different metallicity diagnostic methods, mass-metallicity relation of galaxy, metallicity gradient in quasar host galaxies, BH mass estimation, the effect of different spectral energy distribution (SED) models, and a few other potential sources of uncertainties.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>We propose a possibility that the high metallicity in quasar BLR might be caused by metal enrichment from massive star formation in the nucleus region of quasars or even the accretion disk.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Quasars with bigger black holes or brighter light have more metals in their surrounding gas clouds, and this metal richness stays the same no matter how far away the quasars are. The gas right near these quasars is about two to ten times richer in metals than the galaxies that host them. The researchers checked their methods carefully to make sure these results weren’t just measurement errors. They think that bursts of massive star formation—either very close to the black hole or in the disk of material falling into it—could explain why these regions are so full of metals.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Mobile robots, becoming increasingly autonomous, are capable of operating in diverse and unknown environments.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>This flexibility allows them to fulfill goals independently and adapting their actions dynamically without rigidly predefined control codes.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>However, their autonomous behavior complicates guaranteeing safety and reliability due to the limited influence of a human operator to accurately supervise and verify each robot's actions.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>To ensure autonomous mobile robot's safety and reliability, which are aspects of dependability, methods are needed both in the planning and execution of missions for autonomous mobile robots.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In this article, a twofold approach is presented that ensures fault removal in the context of mission planning and fault prevention during mission execution for autonomous mobile robots.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>First, the approach consists of a concept based on formal verification applied during the planning phase of missions.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Second, the approach consists of a rule-based concept applied during mission execution.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>A use case applying the approach is presented, discussing how the two concepts complement each other and what contribution they make to certain aspects of dependability.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Autonomous robots can explore on their own, but it’s hard to keep them safe when no one can watch every step. This paper introduces two new ideas to solve this. First, it uses a mathematical check on the robot’s mission plan before it starts to catch any mistakes early. Second, it adds a simple rule-based system that watches the robot during its mission and stops things if something goes wrong. Together, these methods find errors before they happen and prevent problems in real time, making self-driving robots much more reliable.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Creating fully annotated labels for medical image segmentation is prohibitively time-intensive and costly, emphasizing the necessity for innovative approaches that minimize reliance on detailed annotations.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Scribble annotations offer a more cost-effective alternative, significantly reducing the expenses associated with full annotations.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>However, scribble annotations offer limited and imprecise information, failing to capture the detailed structural and boundary characteristics necessary for accurate organ delineation.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>To address these challenges, we propose HELPNet, a novel scribble-based weakly supervised segmentation framework, designed to bridge the gap between annotation efficiency and segmentation performance.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>HELPNet integrates three modules.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The Hierarchical perturbations consistency (HPC) module enhances feature learning by employing density-controlled jigsaw perturbations across global, local, and focal views, enabling robust modeling of multi-scale structural representations.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Building on this, the Entropy-guided pseudo-label (EGPL) module evaluates the confidence of segmentation predictions using entropy, generating high-quality pseudo-labels.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Finally, the structural prior refinement (SPR) module incorporates connectivity and bounded priors to enhance the precision and reliability and pseudo-labels.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Experimental results on three public datasets ACDC, MSCMRseg, and CHAOS show that HELPNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods for scribble-based weakly supervised segmentation and achieves performance comparable to fully supervised methods.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>The code is available at https://github.com/IPMI-NWU/HELPNet.</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: HELPNet is a new computer program that learns to spot important regions in medical images using quick scribble marks instead of detailed outlines. This makes training the program much faster and cheaper. It uses three main ideas. First, it mixes small and large patches of the image so it can learn both fine details and overall shapes. Second, it scores its own guesses with a measure called entropy to pick the most reliable “fake” labels when real ones aren’t available. Third, it uses simple rules about how regions stay connected and where their edges should be to clean up its predictions. In tests on public medical image collections, HELPNet beat other weakly supervised methods and performed just as well as models trained with full outlines.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <CONTRIBUTION>We prove a so-called linking theorem and some of its corollaries, namely a mountain pass theorem and a three critical points theorem for Keller $ C^1$-functional on $ C^1 $- Frechet manifolds.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>Our approach relies on a deformation result which is not implemented by considering the negative pseudo-gradient flows.</BACKGROUND><CONTRIBUTION>Furthermore, for mappings between Frechet manifolds we provide a set of sufficient conditions in terms of the Palais–Smale condition that indicates when a local diffeomorphism is a global one.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper proves three big results about finding special points in extremely complex spaces—think of these spaces as giant collections of functions. First, it shows a “linking” method that connects different parts of the space to find a solution. Second, it uses a “mountain pass” idea, imagining you find the lowest high point on a mountain ridge to locate a special point. Third, it guarantees at least three such points exist under certain conditions. Instead of the usual “flow downhill” approach, the authors introduce a fresh way to gently deform the space to reveal these points. They also give clear rules for when a smooth transformation in these spaces can be undone. Together, these tools make it much easier for mathematicians to prove that solutions exist for very hard problems in advanced geometry and analysis.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Spectral kernel methods are techniques for mapping data into a coordinate system that efficiently reveals the geometric structure—in particular, the “connectivity”—of the data.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>These methods depend on tuning parameters.</BACKGROUND><CONTRIBUTION>We analyze the dependence of the method on these tuning parameters.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>We focus on one particular technique—diffusion maps—but our analysis can be used for other spectral methods as well.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>We identify the key population quantities, we define an appropriate risk function for analyzing the estimators, and we explain how these methods relate to classical kernel smoothing.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>We also show that, in some cases, fast rates of convergence are possible even in high dimensions.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>The Appendix of the article is available online as supplementary materials.</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper studies special tools called spectral kernel methods that help find hidden patterns in data by turning it into a new form. The authors focus on one method called diffusion maps but also explain how their ideas work for other similar techniques. They introduce two new ways to check how well these methods work—a set of “population quantities” and a “risk function”—and show how these relate to older ideas in smoothing data. Finally, they prove that, with the right settings, these methods can learn patterns very quickly, even when the data has lots of features.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <CONTRIBUTION>In this expository paper, we provide the readers with an overview of Dennis Sullivan’s major contributions to the area of Dynamical Systems.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Dennis Sullivan was a mathematician who found new ways to study how things change over time. He showed that simple rules can lead to chaotic behavior and created tools to analyze that chaos. He also explained why fractals—those endlessly detailed shapes—have repeating patterns. This article brings together all of Sullivan’s discoveries so students can see how his work helps predict the behavior of complicated systems.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>We have recently seen tremendous progress in realistic text-to-motion generation.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Yet, the existing methods often fail or produce implausible motions with unseen text inputs, which limits the applications.</BACKGROUND><CONTRIBUTION>In this paper, we present OMG, a novel framework, which enables compelling motion generation from zero-shot open-vocabulary text prompts.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>Our key idea is to carefully tailor the pretrain-then-finetune paradigm into the text-to-motion generation.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>At the pre-training stage, our model improves the generation ability by learning the rich out-of-domain inherent motion traits.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>To this end, we scale up a large unconditional diffusion model up to 1B parameters, so as to utilize the massive unlabeled motion data up to over 20M motion instances.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>At the subsequent fine-tuning stage, we introduce motion ControlNet, which incorporates text prompts as conditioning information, through a trainable copy of the pre-trained model and the proposed novel Mixture-of-Controllers (MoC) block.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>MoC block adaptively recognizes various ranges of the sub-motions with a cross-attention mechanism and processes them separately with the text-token-specific experts.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>Such a design effectively aligns the CLIP token embeddings of text prompts to various ranges of compact and expressive motion features.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>Extensive experiments demonstrate that our OMG achieves significant improvements over the state-of-the-art methods on zero-shot text-to-motion generation.</CONTRIBUTION><BACKGROUND>Project page: https://tr3e.github.io/omg-page.</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: OMG is a new computer system that turns any text description into realistic human movement. It works in two steps. First, it learns general motion patterns from more than 20 million examples using a powerful diffusion model. Then it fine-tunes those motions with a special controller that links each word in the text to specific parts of the movement. In tests, OMG produced human motions that were much more lifelike and varied than older methods.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>In the evolution towards the forthcoming era of sixth-generation (6G) mobile communication systems characterized by ubiquitous intelligence, integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is in a phase of burgeoning development.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>However, the capabilities of communication and sensing within single frequency band fall short of meeting the escalating demands.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>To this end, this paper introduces a carrier aggregation (CA)-enabled multi-input multi-output orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) ISAC system fusing the sensing data on high and low-frequency bands by symbol-level fusion for ultimate communication experience and high-accuracy sensing.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>The challenges in sensing signal processing introduced by CA include the initial phase misalignment of the echo signals on high and low-frequency bands due to attenuation and radar cross section, and the fusion of the sensing data on high and low-frequency bands with different physical-layer parameters.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>To this end, the sensing signal processing is decomposed into two stages.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In the first stage, the problem of initial phase misalignment of the echo signals on high and low-frequency bands is solved by the angle compensation, spatial filtering and cyclic cross-correlation operations.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>In the second stage, this paper realizes symbol-level fusion of the sensing data on high and low-frequency bands through sensing vector rearrangement and cyclic prefix adjustment operations, thereby obtaining high-precision sensing performance.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Then, the closed-form communication mutual information (MI) and sensing Cram'er-Rao lower bound (CRLB) for the proposed ISAC system are derived to explore the theoretical performance bound with CA.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Simulation results validate the feasibility and superiority of the proposed ISAC system.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: As 6G wireless networks evolve, we need new tricks to make them faster and smarter. This paper shows how to use both high-pitched and low-pitched radio waves together. First, it fixes out-of-sync echoes by lining up the signals with angle tweaks and pattern matching. Next, it merges this cleaned-up data so devices can send messages faster and “see” their surroundings more clearly. The researchers also work out the ultimate speed and sensing limits of their approach. Finally, computer tests prove their mixed-band method beats older systems that only used one frequency.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>The scale-free (SF) structures that commonly appear in many complex networks are a hot topic in social, biological, and information sciences.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>These self-organized generation mechanisms are expected to be useful for efficient communication or robust connectivity in socio-technological infrastructures.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>This paper is the first review of geographical SF network models.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We discuss the essential generation mechanisms for inducing the structures with power-law behavior, and consider the properties of planarity and link length.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>Distributed design of geographical SF networks without the crossing and long-range links that cause interference and dissipation problems is very important for many applications such as communications, power grids, and sensor systems.</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This work studies networks where a few spots (called nodes) have many connections while most have only a few. The authors show that geography—where those nodes sit on a map—matters a lot. They introduce simple rules that let some nodes become hubs but keep all links short and prevent lines from crossing. They explain how these networks grow over time and how features like planarity (no overlaps) and link length affect how well the network works. Finally, they show how engineers can use these ideas to build reliable systems—like internet links, power grids, or sensor arrays—that stay strong and avoid interference.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>The eclipses of certain types of binary millisecond pulsars (i.e. ‘black widows’ and ‘redbacks’) are often studied using high-time-resolution, ‘beamformed’ radio observations.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>However, they may also be detected in images generated from interferometric data.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>As part of a larger imaging project to characterize the variable and transient sky at radio frequencies $<200,\mathrm{MHz}$, we have blindly detected the redback system PSR~J2215+5135 as a variable source of interest with the Low-Frequency Array (LOFAR).</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Using observations with cadences of two weeks--six months, we find preliminary evidence that the eclipse duration is frequency dependent ($\propto\nu^{-0.4}$), such that the pulsar is eclipsed for longer at lower frequencies, in broad agreement with beamformed studies of other similar sources.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Furthermore, the detection of the eclipses in imaging data suggests an eclipsing medium that absorbs the pulsed emission, rather than scattering it.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Our study is also a demonstration of the prospects of finding pulsars in wide-field imaging surveys with the current generation of low-frequency radio telescopes.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Pulsars are spinning neutron stars that send out regular radio pulses. Instead of using special narrow scans, these scientists used LOFAR—a radio telescope that takes wide‐field sky images—to spot the pulsar PSR J2215+5135. They found that when the pulsar is eclipsed (its signal disappears), the eclipse lasts longer at lower radio frequencies in a simple pattern: lower frequency means a longer eclipse. By watching exactly when the pulses vanished, they showed the radio waves are absorbed by the blocking material, not just scattered away. This work proves that using wide‐field, low‐frequency images is a powerful new way to find and study pulsars.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>In a recent paper the authors studied numerically the hydrogen ground state in stochastic electrodynamics (SED) within the non-relativistic approximation.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>In quantum theory the leading non-relativistic corrections to the ground state energy dominate the Lamb shift related to the photon cloud that should cause the quantum-like behaviour of SED.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>The present work takes these corrections into account in the numerical modelling.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>It is found that they have little effect; the self-ionisation that occurs without them remains present.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>It is speculated that the point-charge approximation for the electron is the cause of the failure.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Scientists built a computer model of the hydrogen atom and added energy corrections from relativity and quantum theory. But in the simulation, the atom still loses its electron—something that doesn’t happen for a real hydrogen atom. The team thinks this happens because they treat the electron as a tiny point with no size. This finding shows that simply adding standard energy corrections isn’t enough. To get a stable atom in the model, they need a more realistic way to describe the electron.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Estimates of population size for hidden and hard-to-reach individuals are of particular interest to health officials when health problems are concentrated in such populations.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Efforts to derive these estimates are often frustrated by a range of factors including social stigma or an association with illegal activities that ordinarily preclude conventional survey strategies.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>This paper builds on and extends prior work that proposed a method to meet these challenges.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Here we describe a rigorous formalization of a one-step, network-based population estimation procedure that can be employed under conditions of anonymity.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The estimation procedure is designed to be implemented alongside currently accepted strategies for research with hidden populations.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Simulation experiments are described that test the efficacy of the method across a range of implementation conditions and hidden population sizes.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The results of these experiments show that reliable population estimates can be derived for hidden, networked population as large as 12,500 and perhaps larger for one family of random graphs.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>As such, the method shows potential for cost-effective implementation health and disease surveillance officials concerned with hidden populations.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>Limitations and future work are discussed in the concluding section.</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Researchers found a way to count people in hidden groups—like those at risk for a disease—without asking for anyone’s name. You only need one simple question: “How many people do you know in that group?” This fits right into the surveys scientists already use. In computer tests, it gave accurate counts for groups as big as about 12,500 people. Because it never asks for names but still works well, it’s cheap and easy to run. Now researchers have a private, reliable tool to study health issues in communities that are hard to reach.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>A spacelike surface with cylinder topology can be described by various sets of canonical variables within pure AdS3 gravity.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Each is made of one real coordinate and one real momentum.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>The Hamiltonian can be either H = 0 or it can be nonzero and we display the canonical transformations that map one into the other, in two relevant cases.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>In a choice of canonical coordinates, one of them is the cylinder aspect q, which evolves nontrivially in time.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>The time dependence of the aspect is an analytic function of time t and an “angular momentum” J.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>By analytic continuation in both t and J we obtain a Euclidean evolution that can be described geometrically as the motion of a cylinder inside the region of the 3D hyperbolic space bounded by two “domes” (i.e. half spheres), which is topologically a solid torus.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We find that for a given J the Euclidean evolution cannot connect an initial aspect to an arbitrary final aspect; moreover, there are infinitely many Euclidean trajectories that connect any two allowed initial and final aspects.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We compute the transition amplitude in two independent ways; first by solving exactly the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, then by summing in a sensible way all the saddle contributions, and we discuss why both approaches are mutually consistent.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper studies a doughnut-shaped surface floating in curved space. The authors show two different ways to describe this shape and how to switch between them. They use a math trick to find out which starting and ending shapes can connect—and it turns out each allowed pair can change in infinitely many ways. Finally, they work out how likely each shape change is in two ways: by solving a basic physics equation and by looking at key “saddle” shapes in the geometry. Both approaches agree, so their result is solid.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>It is known that spectral networks naturally induce certain coordinate systems on moduli spaces of flat SL(K)-connections on surfaces, previously studied by Fock and Goncharov.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We give a self-contained account of this story in the case K = 2 and explain how it can be extended to incorporate the complexified Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>As we review, the key ingredient in the story is a procedure for passing between moduli of flat SL(2)-connections on C (equipped with a little extra structure) and moduli of equivariant GL(1)-connections over a covering Σ→C; taking holonomies of the equivariant GL(1)-connections then gives the desired coordinate systems on moduli of SL(2)-connections.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>There are two special types of spectral network, related to ideal triangulations and pants decompositions of C; these two types of network lead to Fock–Goncharov and complexified Fenchel–Nielsen coordinate systems, respectively.</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper shows how to use something called spectral networks to create special coordinate systems on surfaces. First, it covers the simplest example, then it explains a more advanced version called complexified Fenchel–Nielsen coordinates. The authors make it easy by showing how to switch between two ways of describing a surface’s twists and turns—one with small matrices and one with number labels on a covering space. Finally, they look at two main types of spectral networks: one made by breaking the surface into triangles and another by cutting it into three-holed pieces. Each type gives its own helpful coordinate system for studying the shape.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Let X be a toric Calabi–Yau 3-fold and let $L\subset X$ be an Aganagic-Vafa outer brane.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We prove two versions of open WDVV equations for the open Gromov–Witten theory of $(X,L)$.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The first version of the open WDVV equation leads to the construction of a semi-simple (formal) Frobenius manifold, and the second version leads to the construction of a flat (formal) F-manifold.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper introduces two new equations (called the open WDVV equations) that explain how certain 3D shapes with a special outer layer (a “brane”) behave. From these equations, the authors build two helpful tools—one they call a Frobenius manifold and the other a flat F-manifold. These tools act like machines that quickly count and study important numbers (open Gromov–Witten invariants), which tell us how many ways curves can fit inside those shapes.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <CONTRIBUTION>We prove the existence of positive solutions with optimal local regularity to homogeneous elliptic equations of Schr"{o}dinger type, under only a form boundedness assumption on $\sigma\in D'(\Omega)$ and an ellipticity assumption on $\mathcal{A}\in L^\infty(\Omega)^{n\times n}$, for an arbitrary open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbf{R}^n$.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We demonstrate that there is a two way correspondence between the form boundedness and the existence of positive solutions to this equation, as well as weak solutions to certain elliptic equations with quadratic nonlinearity in the gradient.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>As a consequence, we obtain necessary and sufficient conditions for both the form‐boundedness (with a sharp upper form bound) and the positivity of the quadratic form of the Schr"{o}dinger type operator with arbitrary distributional potential $\sigma\in D'(\Omega)$, and give examples clarifying the relationship between these two properties.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper looks at a wide range of equations—like the ones used in quantum physics—and shows that you can always find solutions that stay positive and are very smooth if a certain simple condition on the “potential” part of the equation holds. The authors prove that this condition is not just useful but exactly what you need to get those nice solutions. They also show how the same requirement guarantees the related energy stays positive. To make everything clear, they include easy examples that demonstrate how the smooth solutions and the potential condition go hand in hand.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Since late 2019, COVID-19 has quickly emerged as the newest biomedical domain, resulting in a surge of new information.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>As with other emergent domains, the discussion surrounding the topic has been rapidly changing, leading to the spread of misinformation.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>This has created the need for a public space for users to ask questions and receive credible, scientific answers.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>To fulfill this need, we turn to the task of open-domain question-answering, which we can use to efficiently find answers to free-text questions from a large set of documents.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In this work, we present such a system for the emergent domain of COVID-19.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Despite the small data size available, we are able to successfully train the system to retrieve answers from a large-scale corpus of published COVID-19 scientific papers.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Furthermore, we incorporate effective re-ranking and question-answering techniques, such as document diversity and multiple answer spans.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Our open-domain question-answering system can further act as a model for the quick development of similar systems that can be adapted and modified for other developing emergent domains.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: We built a system that can answer questions by searching through many COVID-19 research papers, even though we started with very little data. First, it picks the most relevant documents and then re-ranks them to favor the best matches. Next, it makes sure the selected papers cover different viewpoints instead of repeating the same info. Finally, it finds several spots in those papers where the answer appears, so it’s more likely to be right. This setup is easy to adapt to new topics, letting anyone get fast, trustworthy scientific answers as new research comes out.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Chandrasekaran, Chertkov, Gamarnik, Shah, and Shin recently proved that the average number of independent sets of random regular graphs of size n and degree 3 approaches w^n for large n, where w is approximately 1.54563, consistent with the Bethe approximation.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>They also made the surprising conjecture that the fluctuations of the logarithm of the number of independent sets were only O(1) as n grew large, which would mean that the Bethe approximation is amazingly accurate for all 3-regular graphs.</BACKGROUND><CONTRIBUTION>Here, I provide numerical evidence supporting this conjecture obtained from exact counts of independent sets using binary decision diagrams.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>I also provide numerical evidence that supports the novel conjectures that the number of kernels of 3-regular graphs of size n is given by y^n, where y is approximately 1.299, and that the fluctuations in the logarithm of the number of kernels is also only O(1).</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Imagine a network where every dot (node) connects to exactly three other dots. One thing you can count in such a network is how many ways you can choose dots so that none of them touch each other—these are called independent sets. Using precise computer checks, the authors show that every time you add a new dot, the total number of independent sets multiplies by the same fixed amount, with almost no ups and downs. They also look at another kind of special dot‐group called a kernel (where each dot is either chosen or touches a chosen dot) and find that kernels, too, grow by their own fixed factor for each extra dot, again with very tiny fluctuations. In other words, the simple formulas people guessed for how these counts should grow turn out to be spot-on.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ which has multiplicative reduction at a fixed prime $p$.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>For each positive integer $n$ we put $K_n:=\mathbb{Q}(E[p^n])$.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>The aim of this paper is to extend the author's previous results concerning the order of the $p$-Sylow group of the ideal class group of $K_n$ to a more general setting.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We also modify the previous lower bound of the order and describe the new lower bound in terms of the Mordell–Weil rank of $E(\mathbb{Q})$ and the ramification related to $E$.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper explores a special kind of number system you get by starting with all fractions and then adding certain points from an elliptic curve—points that disappear when you multiply them by powers of a prime number 𝑝. The authors show that earlier results about these systems actually work in more cases than we thought. They also find a better lower limit for the size of an important subgroup inside these systems. It turns out this new limit depends only on two simple facts: how many rational solutions the curve already has and how the curve behaves at the prime 𝑝.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>We explore the predictions of the standard hierarchical clustering scenario, regarding the numbers and metallicities of PopIII stars found within our Galaxy today.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>An analytic, extended Press–Schechter formalism is used to get the mass functions of halos which will host PopIII stars at a given redshift, and which will end up in the Milky Way (MW) today.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Each of these is modeled as a mini galaxy, with a detailed treatment of the dark halo structure, angular momentum distribution, final gas temperature and disk instabilities, all of which determine the fraction of the baryons which are subject to star formation.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Use of new primordial metallicity stellar evolutionary models allows us to trace the history of the stars formed and give accurate estimates of their expected numbers today.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>A first comparison with observational data suggests that the IMF of the first stars was increasingly high mass weighted towards high redshifts, leveling off at z ≈ 9 at a characteristic stellar mass scale mₛ = 10–15 M⊙.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>Details can be found in Hernandez & Ferrara (2001).</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Scientists used new computer models of how stars live and change to figure out how many metal-free “Pop III” stars should still be in our galaxy. They then checked these predictions against real telescope data. They found that the very first stars were mostly huge—about 10 to 15 times the mass of our Sun—and that by the time the universe was about 500 million years old (around redshift nine), this pattern had settled down. These results give us a clearer picture of how the Milky Way’s very first stars formed and grew

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Face recognition systems are widely deployed in safety-critical applications, including law enforcement, yet they exhibit bias across a range of socio-demographic dimensions, such as gender and race.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Conventional wisdom dictates that model biases arise from biased training data.</BACKGROUND><BACKGROUND>As a consequence, previous works on bias mitigation largely focused on pre-processing the training data, adding penalties to prevent bias from effecting the model during training, or post-processing predictions to debias them, yet these approaches have shown limited success on hard problems such as face recognition.</BACKGROUND><CONTRIBUTION>In our work, we discover that biases are actually inherent to neural network architectures themselves.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>Following this reframing, we conduct the first neural architecture search for fairness, jointly with a search for hyperparameters.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>Our search outputs a suite of models which Pareto-dominate all other high-performance architectures and existing bias mitigation methods in terms of accuracy and fairness, often by large margins, on the two most widely used datasets for face identification, CelebA and VGGFace2.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>Furthermore, these models generalize to other datasets and sensitive attributes.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>We release our code, models and raw data files at https://github.com/dooleys/FR-NAS.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper shows that unfair results in face recognition come not just from the data but from how neural networks are built. The authors created the first way to search for network designs that focus on fairness as well as accuracy. Their new models are both more correct and less biased on major face-recognition datasets. These fair designs also work well on completely new datasets and different facial traits. To help others, the researchers have shared all their code and data so anyone can use and improve their work.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Compensated isocurvature perturbations (CIPs) are relative density perturbations in which a baryon-density fluctuation is accompanied by a dark matter density fluctuation such that the total-matter density is unperturbed.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>These fluctuations can be produced primordially if multiple fields are present during inflation, and therefore they can be used to differentiate between different models for the early Universe.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Kinetic Sunyaev–Zeldovich (kSZ) tomography allows for the reconstruction of the radial-velocity field of matter as a function of redshift.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>This technique can be used to reconstruct the total-matter-overdensity field, independent of the galaxy-density field obtained from large-scale galaxy surveys.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We leverage the ability to measure the galaxy- and matter-overdensity fields independently to construct a minimum-variance estimator for the primordial CIP amplitude, based on a mode-by-mode comparison of the two measurements.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We forecast that a configuration corresponding to CMB-S4 and VRO will be able to detect (at $2\sigma$) a CIP amplitude $A$ (for a scale-invariant power spectrum) as small as $A\simeq 5\times 10^{-9}$.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Similarly, a configuration corresponding to SO and DESI will be sensitive to a CIP amplitude $A\simeq 1\times 10^{-7}$.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>These values are to be compared to current constraints $A \leq {\cal O}(0.01)$. </CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Scientists have come up with a new way to find tiny ripples from the early universe called CIPs. They do this by comparing two “maps” of matter: one made by counting galaxies and another made by seeing how galaxy clusters leave faint marks on the cosmic microwave background. The team built a tool that mixes these two maps to measure exactly how strong those ripples are. Their forecasts show that future projects—like the CMB-S4 telescope together with the Vera Rubin Observatory and DESI—could spot ripples billions of times fainter than what we can see today.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Stirling numbers of the first kind are used in the derivation of several population genetics statistics, which in turn are useful for testing evolutionary hypotheses directly from DNA sequences.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Here, we explore the cumulative distribution function of these Stirling numbers, which enables a single direct estimate of the sum, using representations in terms of the incomplete beta function.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>This estimator enables an improved method for calculating an asymptotic estimate for one useful statistic, Fu’s Fs.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>By reducing the calculation from a sum of terms involving Stirling numbers to a single estimate, we simultaneously improve accuracy and dramatically increase speed.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Geneticists often need to add up special math numbers called Stirling numbers to study DNA, but doing this can be slow. The authors found a shortcut using a math formula called the incomplete beta function, which makes those sums much faster. They used this trick to speed up the calculation of Fu’s Fs, a key number that tracks how DNA changes in populations. This new method is both quicker and more accurate. As a result, researchers can test ideas about evolution with DNA data much more efficiently.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>We prove the following results for toric Deligne–Mumford stacks, under minimal compactness hypotheses:</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>The Localization Theorem in equivariant K-theory; the equivariant Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem; the Fourier–Mukai transformation associated to a crepant toric wall-crossing gives an equivariant derived equivalence.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper looks at a special kind of shape that has built-in mirror-like patterns. The authors prove three big things about these shapes when they’re “nicely packed” and don’t go off to infinity. First, they show you can do a hard calculation by splitting it into smaller pieces and still keep track of all the patterns. Second, they update a classic counting rule (called the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch formula) so it works for these shapes, making it much easier to find key numbers. Third, they show that when you change one shape into a closely related one, a process called the Fourier–Mukai transform creates an exact match between how you describe them. Together, these ideas give mathematicians simple new ways to compute important properties and see hidden links between these complex shapes.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Writing assistance is an application closely related to human life and is also a fundamental Natural Language Processing (NLP) research field.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Its aim is to improve the correctness and quality of input texts, with character checking being crucial in detecting and correcting wrong characters.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>From the perspective of the real world where handwriting occupies the vast majority, characters that humans get wrong include faked characters (i.e., untrue characters created due to writing errors) and misspelled characters (i.e., true characters used incorrectly due to spelling errors).</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>However, existing datasets and related studies only focus on misspelled characters mainly caused by phonological or visual confusion, thereby ignoring faked characters which are more common and difficult.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>To break through this dilemma, we present Visual-C$^3$, a human-annotated Visual Chinese Character Checking dataset with faked and misspelled Chinese characters.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>To the best of our knowledge, Visual-C$^3$ is the first real-world visual and the largest human-crafted dataset for the Chinese character checking scenario.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Additionally, we also propose and evaluate novel baseline methods on Visual-C$^3$.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Extensive empirical results and analyses show that Visual-C$^3$ is high-quality yet challenging.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The Visual-C$^3$ dataset and the baseline methods will be publicly available to facilitate further research in the community.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Visual-C³ is a new, large dataset that helps computers find and fix fake or misspelled Chinese characters in handwritten notes. It’s the first dataset of its size for this task. The authors also created and tested basic computer models on Visual-C³. They found that, even though the dataset is really helpful, current systems still struggle with some of its challenges. By sharing the dataset and their code online, they hope other researchers can build better writing-help tools in the future.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>With the improvements in generative models, the issues of producing hallucinations in various domains (e.g., law, writing) have been brought to people’s attention due to concerns about misinformation.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>In this paper, we focus on neural fake news, which refers to content generated by neural networks aiming to mimic the style of real news to deceive people.</BACKGROUND><CONTRIBUTION>To prevent harmful disinformation spreading fallaciously from malicious social media (e.g., content farms), we propose a novel verification framework, Style-News, using publisher metadata to imply a publisher’s template with the corresponding text types, political stance, and credibility.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Based on threat modeling aspects, a style-aware neural news generator is introduced as an adversary for generating news content conditioning for a specific publisher, and style and source discriminators are trained to defend against this attack by identifying which publisher the style corresponds with, and discriminating whether the source of the given news is human-written or machine-generated.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>To evaluate the quality of the generated content, we integrate various dimensional metrics (language fluency, content preservation, and style adherence) and demonstrate that Style-News significantly outperforms the previous approaches by a margin of 0.35 for fluency, 15.24 for content, and 0.38 for style at most.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Moreover, our discriminative model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of publisher prediction (up to 4.64%) and neural fake news detection (+6.94% 31.72%).</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>We plan to release our Style-News publicly, with the aim of improving neural fake news detection.</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Style-News is a new system that learns how different news outlets write so it can both copy their style and spot AI-written fakes. It trains two tools: one that writes realistic-sounding articles in a publisher’s style, and another that detects when an article was made by a machine. In tests, Style-News beat older methods on writing quality, accuracy of facts, and its ability to catch fake news. The authors have shared Style-News publicly so everyone can use it to find AI-generated articles more reliably.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Black holes and wormholes are solutions of Einstein's field equations, both of which, from afar, can look like a central mass.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We show here that although at large distances both behave like Newtonian objects, close to the event horizon or to the throat, black holes and wormholes have different tidal effects on stars, due to their respective geometries.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We quantify this difference by a numerical procedure in the Schwarzschild black hole and the exponential wormhole backgrounds, and compare the peak fallback rates of tidal debris in these geometries.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The tidal disruption rates in these backgrounds are also computed.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>It is shown that these quantities are a few times higher for wormholes, compared to the black hole cases.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This study explains that black holes and wormholes, though they seem the same from far away, actually pull stars apart in different ways when you get close. Using computer simulations, the researchers measured how often stars break up and how much debris falls back near both Schwarzschild black holes and exponential-model wormholes. They found wormholes cause a few times more stellar disruption and debris return than black holes, suggesting a clear method to tell these exotic objects apart.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Motivated by the recent synthesis of the spin-1 A-site spinel NiRh_{2}O_{4}, we investigate the classical to quantum crossover of a frustrated J_{1}-J_{2} Heisenberg model on the diamond lattice upon varying the spin length S.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Applying a recently developed pseudospin functional renormalization group approach for arbitrary spin-S magnets, we find that systems with S\ge 3/2 reside in the classical regime, where the low-temperature physics is dominated by the formation of coplanar spirals and a thermal (order-by-disorder) transition.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>For smaller local moments S=1 or S=\tfrac12, we find that the system evades a thermal ordering transition and forms a quantum spiral spin liquid where the fluctuations are restricted to characteristic momentum-space surfaces.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>For the tetragonal phase of NiRh_{2}O_{4}, a modified J_{1}-J_{2}^{-}-J_{2}^{\perp} exchange model is found to favor a conventionally ordered N'eel state (for arbitrary spin S), even in the presence of a strong local single-ion spin anisotropy, and it requires additional sources of frustration to explain the experimentally observed absence of a thermal ordering transition.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Scientists used a new computer method to study a diamond‐shaped crystal called NiRh₂O₄. Inside this material, each atom has a tiny magnetic moment, or “spin.” They found that when these spins are large—equal to 3/2 or more—they lock into neat spiral patterns at very low temperatures. But if the spins are smaller—1 or 1/2—they don’t freeze; instead, they stay in a flowing, liquid‐like state called a “quantum spiral spin liquid.” The team also discovered that in the real NiRh₂O₄ crystal, extra “frustration” (competing forces) is needed to keep the spins from lining up. This explains why experiments never see the spins suddenly freeze as the material cools

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <CONTRIBUTION>We show that recent multivariate generalizations of the Araki–Lieb–Thirring inequality and the Golden–Thompson inequality (Sutter et al. in Commun Math Phys, 2016. doi:10.1007/s00220-016-2778-5) for Schatten norms hold more generally for all unitarily invariant norms and certain variations thereof.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The main technical contribution is a generalization of the concept of log-majorization which allows us to treat majorization with regard to logarithmic integral averages of vectors of singular values.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper looks at two important rules about how “big” different parts of a grid of numbers (a matrix) can be. Until now, these rules only worked for one specific way of measuring size. The authors prove that the same rules actually hold true for many other size measures, so they apply much more broadly. They also come up with a new, easy-to-use way to compare the sizes of different parts of the matrix by taking the average on a logarithmic scale (think of it like measuring earthquakes on the Richter scale). Together, these breakthroughs let mathematicians use and prove these matrix rules in more places and with simpler methods.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Two aspects required to establish a planning in orthognatic surgery are addressed in this paper.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>First, a 3D cephalometric analysis, which is clinically essential for the therapeutic decision.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Then, an original method to build a biomechanical model of patient face soft tissue, which provides evaluation of the aesthetic outcomes of an intervention.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>Both points are developed within a clinical application context for computer aided maxillofacial surgery.</BACKGROUND> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Surgeons can now plan jaw surgery with two computer steps in one program. First, they build a 3D model of the patient’s skull to see exactly how the bones will move. Then, they use a new soft-tissue simulator that predicts how the skin and muscles will shift, so they can preview the patient’s new face before the operation. By combining both steps into easy-to-use clinical software, doctors get more accurate surgery plans and safer results for their patients.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Prohibited item detection is crucial for ensuring public safety, yet current X-ray image-based detection methods often lack comprehensive data-driven exploration.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>This paper introduces a novel data augmentation approach tailored for prohibited item detection, leveraging unique characteristics inherent to X-ray imagery.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>Our method is motivated by observations of physical properties including: 1) X-ray Transmission Imagery: Unlike reflected light images, transmitted X-ray pixels represent composite information from multiple materials along the imaging path.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Material-based Pseudo-coloring: Pseudo-color rendering in X-ray images correlates directly with material properties, aiding in material distinction.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Building on a novel perspective from physical properties, we propose a simple yet effective X-ray image augmentation technique, Background Mixup (BGM), for prohibited item detection in security screening contexts.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The essence is the rich background simulation of X-ray images to induce the model to increase its attention to the foreground.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The approach introduces 1) contour information of baggage and 2) variation of material information into the original image by Mixup at patch level.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Background Mixup is plug-and-play, parameter-free, highly generalizable and provides an effective solution to the limitations of classical visual augmentations in non-reflected light imagery.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>When implemented with different high-performance detectors, our augmentation method consistently boosts performance across diverse X-ray datasets from various devices and environments.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses strong baselines while maintaining similar training resources.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This study presents Background Mixup (BGM), a simple trick for improving X-ray baggage scans. BGM mixes in parts of different bag backgrounds and adds color hints for materials so that computer programs learn to pay more attention to the items they need to find. It works by blending small patches of bag shapes and “fake” colors for different materials. Tests on several X-ray datasets show that using BGM makes these programs better at spotting forbidden items—and it does so without needing extra training time or more data.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Burgers-Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) scaling has recently (re-) surfaced in a variety of physical contexts, ranging from anharmonic chains to quantum systems such as open superfluids, in which a variety of random forces may be encountered and/or engineered.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Motivated by these developments, we here provide a generalization of the KPZ universality class to situations with long-ranged temporal correlations in the noise, which purposefully break the Galilean invariance that is central to the conventional KPZ solution.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We compute the phase diagram and critical exponents of the KPZ equation with 1/f noise (KPZ1/f) in spatial dimensions 1≤d<4 using the dynamic renormalization group with a frequency cutoff technique in a one-loop truncation.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Distinct features of KPZ1/f are (i) a generically scale-invariant, rough phase at high noise levels that violates fluctuation-dissipation relations and exhibits hyperthermal statistics even in d=1, (ii) a fine-tuned roughening transition at which the flow fulfills an emergent thermal-like fluctuation-dissipation relation, that separates the rough phase from (iii) a massive phase in 1<d<4 (in d=1 the interface is always rough).</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We point out potential connections to nonlinear hydrodynamics with a reduced set of conservation laws and noisy quantum liquids.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Scientists took a well-known physics model and added a special kind of time-varying noise that breaks one of the model’s usual balance rules. Then they used math to explore how this “noisy” model behaves in spaces of one, two, three, and four dimensions. They found three distinct behaviors: a rough phase where the normal balance rules no longer apply, a transition point where the usual rules briefly reappear, and a smooth phase in higher dimensions. These discoveries give researchers new tools for studying complex fluid flows and certain advanced quantum systems.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Good tools can bring mechanical verification to programs written in mainstream functional languages.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>We use hs-to-coq to translate significant portions of Haskell's containers library into Coq, and verify it against specifications that we derive from a variety of sources including type class laws, the library's test suite, and interfaces from Coq's standard library.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Our work shows that it is feasible to verify mature, widely-used, highly optimized, and unmodified Haskell code.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We also learn more about the theory of weight-balanced trees, extend hs-to-coq to handle partiality, and -- since we found no bugs -- attest to the superb quality of well-tested functional code.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper shows how you can use one program to prove that another program works correctly. The authors picked a popular Haskell library and used a tool called hs-to-coq to turn its code into Coq, which is a system for checking proofs. They ran the library’s existing tests inside Coq and used Coq’s logic rules to verify every function. They also upgraded hs-to-coq so it can handle parts of the code that aren’t always defined. Along the way, they discovered new facts about special tree structures. In the end, they found no mistakes, proving that well-tested functional code can be trusted to be correct.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Disinformation through fake news is an ongoing problem in our society and has become easily spread through social media.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>The most cost- and time-effective way to filter these large amounts of data is to use a combination of human and technical interventions to identify it.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>From a technical perspective, Natural Language Processing (NLP) is widely used in detecting fake news.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Social media companies use NLP techniques to identify the fake news and warn their users, but fake news may still slip through undetected.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>It is especially a problem in more localised contexts (outside the United States of America).</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>How do we adjust fake news detection systems to work better for local contexts such as in South Africa.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>In this work we investigate fake news detection on South African websites.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We curate a dataset of South African fake news and then train detection models.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We contrast this with using widely available fake news datasets (from mostly USA website).</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>We also explore making the datasets more diverse by combining them and observe the differences in behaviour in writing between nations’ fake news using interpretable machine learning.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: The researchers gathered news articles from South African websites and trained computer models to spot fake news there. They then compared these models to ones built mostly on U.S. news and used special tools to see how writing styles differ. Their tests showed that tailoring fake-news detectors to local sources and mixing in diverse data makes the systems more accurate and easier to understand for each region.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>No abstract given.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>Contents: I. Definition and Introduction</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>II. Schelling Model</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>III. Opinion Dynamics</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>IV. Languages, Hierarchies and Football</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>V. Future Directions</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper doesn’t start with the usual summary but instead first gives all the basic definitions and an introduction. Next, it explains the Schelling model, which shows how people’s opinions can shift when they interact. After that, it looks at real-world uses, like how languages spread, how social groups form, and even how fans behave at football games. Finally, the authors suggest new research questions and ideas to help future studies in sociophysics, pointing the way toward fresh experiments and models.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <CONTRIBUTION>We report on a pilot study of a novel observing technique, defocused transmission spectroscopy, and its application to the study of exoplanet atmospheres using ground-based platforms.</CONTRIBUTION> <BACKGROUND>Similar to defocused photometry, defocused transmission spectroscopy has an added advantage over normal spectroscopy in that it reduces systematic errors due to flat-fielding, point spread function variations, slit-jaw imperfections and other effects associated with ground-based observations.</BACKGROUND><CONTRIBUTION>For one of the planetary systems studied, WASP-12b, we report a tentative detection of additional Na absorption of 0.12 ± 0.03[+0.03] per cent during transit using a 2 Å wavelength mask.</CONTRIBUTION><CONTRIBUTION>After consideration of a systematic that occurs mid-transit, it is likely that the true depth is actually closer to 0.15 per cent.</CONTRIBUTION><BACKGROUND>This is a similar level of absorption reported in the atmosphere of HD 209458b (0.135 ± 0.017 per cent; Snellen et al. 2008).</BACKGROUND><CONTRIBUTION>Finally, we outline methods that will improve the technique during future observations, based on our findings from this pilot study.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Scientists developed a new method called defocused transmission spectroscopy to study the atmospheres of planets outside our solar system with fewer errors. They tried it on the planet WASP-12b and detected extra sodium gas, which blocked about 0.15% more starlight when the planet passed in front of its star. Finally, they suggest simple improvements—like better calibration and watching the planet for longer—to make this technique even more reliable for future studies.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>The potential of integrating public transit with ridesharing includes shorter travel time for commuters and higher occupancy rate of personal vehicles and public transit ridership.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>In this paper, we describe a centralized transit system that integrates public transit and ridesharing to reduce travel time for commuters.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>In the system, a set of ridesharing providers (drivers) and a set of public transit riders are received.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>The optimization goal of the system is to assign riders to drivers by arranging public transit and ridesharing combined routes subject to shorter commuting time for as many riders as possible.</BACKGROUND><CONTRIBUTION>We give an exact algorithm, which is an ILP formulation based on a hypergraph representation of the problem.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>By using the ILP and the hypergraph, we give approximation algorithms based on LP-rounding and hypergraph matching/weighted set packing, respectively.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>As a case study, we conduct an extensive computational study based on real-world public transit dataset and ridesharing dataset in Chicago city.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>To evaluate the effectiveness of the transit system and our algorithms, we generate data instances from the datasets.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The experimental results show that more than 60% of riders are assigned to drivers on average, riders' commuting time is reduced by 23% and vehicle occupancy rate is improved to almost 3.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Our proposed algorithms are efficient for practical scenarios.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: This paper builds a system that uses both buses/trains and shared rides to help people travel faster. It creates a precise algorithm and simpler approximation methods to match riders with drivers, and tests these on Chicago data, finding that it cuts travel time by 23%, matches over 60% of riders, and boosts vehicle use to nearly three people per trip. These findings show their methods work well in real life.

column2: <TASK> Summarize this abstract for high-school audience while highlight importance of contributions </TASK> <ABSTRACT> <BACKGROUND>Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) are bright extragalactic sources with X-ray luminosities above 10^39 erg/s powered by accretion onto compact objects.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>According to the first studies performed with XMM-Newton ULXs seemed to be excellent candidates to host intermediate-mass black holes (10^2-4 solar masses).</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>However, in the last years the interpretation of super-Eddington accretion onto stellar-mass black holes or neutron stars for most ULXs has gained a strong consensus.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>One critical missing piece to confirm the super-Eddington scenario was the direct detection of the massive, radiatively-driven winds expected as atomic emission/absorption lines in ULX spectra.</BACKGROUND> <BACKGROUND>The first evidence for winds was found as residuals in the soft X-ray spectra of ULXs.</BACKGROUND> <CONTRIBUTION>Most recently we have been able to resolve these residuals into rest-frame emission and blueshifted (~0.2c) absorption lines arising from highly ionized gas in the deep high-resolution XMM-Newton spectra of two ultraluminous X-ray sources.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>The compact object is therefore surrounded by powerful ultrafast winds as predicted by models of hyper-Eddington accretion.</CONTRIBUTION> <CONTRIBUTION>Here we discuss the relevance of these discoveries and the importance of further, deep, XMM-Newton observations of powerful winds in many other ultraluminous X-ray sources to estimate the energetics of the wind, the geometry of the system, and the masses of the central accretors.</CONTRIBUTION> </ABSTRACT>
column3: Scientists used the XMM-Newton space telescope to spot incredibly fast winds coming from ultraluminous X-ray sources—objects so bright they outshine whole galaxies in X-rays. These winds race out at nearly one-fifth the speed of light and carry huge amounts of ionized gas away from the source. This finding shows that these powerful X-ray sources don’t just shine—they blast out massive gas flows. To learn more, the researchers say we need longer, more detailed observations to figure out exactly how much energy these winds carry, what shape they have, and how big the hidden, compact objects powering them really are.
